11200:
Nyctophobia (noun) is an intense, irrational, and overwhelming fear of darkness or the night. It is a specific type of phobia — which means it is not just a general discomfort or mild unease, but a recognized psychological condition where the fear is extreme enough to disrupt a person's normal life.

The key word here is irrational. A person with nyctophobia knows, deep down, that darkness itself cannot harm them. Yet their mind and body react as though they are in serious danger the moment lights go out or night falls.
The Difference Between Normal Fear and Nyctophobia

Almost everyone feels a little uneasy in complete darkness at some point — it is a basic human instinct, because in the dark, we cannot see threats. That is perfectly normal.

Nyctophobia is different. The fear goes far beyond normal caution. Here is how to tell them apart:

A person who is normally cautious in the dark might feel a bit nervous walking through an unlit alley at night, turn on a lamp before entering a dark room, and then move on with their life without a second thought.

A person with nyctophobia might refuse to sleep without every light on, be unable to enter a dark room at all, feel their heart race and body shake at the mere thought of darkness, and experience this fear consistently — not just once in a while.

The defining line is this: normal fear is a passing reaction to a real situation; nyctophobia is a persistent, powerful fear that is out of proportion to any actual danger, and it interferes with everyday functioning.
What a Person with Nyctophobia Actually Experiences

When someone with nyctophobia encounters darkness — or even anticipates it — their body launches a full stress response, as if a real physical threat is present. This is called the fight-or-flight response. Their brain misreads darkness as danger and sounds the alarm.

This can cause the following to happen all at once, physically and mentally:

The physical side includes a rapidly pounding heart, shortness of breath, sweating, trembling or shaking, a dry mouth, chest tightness, dizziness, and even nausea. The body is genuinely preparing to either fight a threat or flee from one — even though no real threat exists.

The mental and emotional side includes an overwhelming sense of dread or doom, a feeling that something terrible is about to happen, the inability to think clearly or calm down, and sometimes a complete panic attack — which is a sudden, intense wave of fear that peaks within minutes and feels absolutely terrifying while it lasts.

Importantly, the person usually knows their fear is excessive. This awareness, however, does not make the fear go away. That is part of what makes phobias so frustrating.

Nyctophobia is especially common in children. It is, in fact, one of the most common childhood fears in the world. Young children's minds are still developing and are very active with imagination — darkness becomes a space where their minds fill in frightening things that are not really there (monsters under the bed, shadows in the corner, unknown figures, etc.).

For most children, this fear naturally fades as they grow older and better understand the world around them.

However, in some people, the fear does not fade — it carries into adolescence and adulthood. Nyctophobia can also first develop in adulthood, often triggered by a traumatic or frightening experience that happened in the dark (an attack, an accident, getting lost, witnessing something disturbing at night, etc.). Once the brain links darkness with extreme danger, it can become very hard to undo that link without help.

Nyctophobia affects people of all genders and backgrounds, though it tends to be more commonly reported in children and in individuals who are generally prone to anxiety.

The causes of nyctophobia are not always the same for every person. Generally, they fall into a few broad categories:

Learned fear — A child who is repeatedly told that the dark is dangerous, or who sees a parent or caregiver react with extreme fear to darkness, may absorb that fear and develop it themselves. The brain learns that darkness = threat.

A traumatic experience — If something frightening happened to a person in the dark (a break-in, an accident, getting separated from family at night, being trapped somewhere dark), the brain can create a powerful association between darkness and that terror. Even long after the event is over, darkness continues to trigger the fear.

Generalized anxiety — People who already have anxiety disorders are more vulnerable to developing specific phobias like nyctophobia, because their nervous systems are already primed to detect and react to threats.

The imagination factor — Darkness removes visual information. The human brain, especially a young or anxious brain, has a tendency to fill that information gap with threats. Over time, this habit of imagining threats in the dark can deepen into a full phobia.

Nyctophobia can quietly take over many parts of a person's routine. A person living with it might sleep with every light on, run up high electricity bills because lights are never switched off, be unable to watch a movie at a cinema, refuse to attend evening outdoor events, feel anxious hours before sunset, and struggle with sleep — since night naturally means darkness. Their relationships, work, and mental health can all be affected as a result.

Children with nyctophobia often refuse to sleep in their own room, want a parent to stay with them all night, or have frequent nightmares or sleep disturbances.

Nyctophobia is highly treatable. People do not have to live with it forever. The most effective approaches are psychological, and they work by teaching the brain a new response to darkness.

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) is the most widely used and effective treatment. A therapist helps the person identify the irrational thoughts fueling their fear ("darkness means I will be hurt") and replace them with realistic ones ("darkness is simply the absence of light; I am safe"). Over time, the brain learns to stop interpreting darkness as a threat.

Exposure Therapy is often used alongside CBT. It involves very gradually and safely exposing the person to darkness — starting with something mild, like dimming the lights slightly, then gradually increasing the level of darkness over many sessions. Each small step teaches the brain: "I was in the dark, and nothing bad happened." This slowly dismantles the fear.

Relaxation techniques such as controlled breathing and mindfulness help the person manage the physical symptoms of panic when they arise.

For children, gentle, patient reassurance from caregivers combined with a slow introduction to sleeping in low light (using a small nightlight and gradually reducing it over time) can be very effective.
Using the Word in a Sentence

To cement your understanding, here is how the word "nyctophobia" appears naturally in sentences:

  • Her nyctophobia was so severe that she kept every room in her home brightly lit, even while she slept.
  • After years of therapy, Marcus finally overcame his nyctophobia and was able to sit comfortably in a dark cinema for the first time.
  • Nyctophobia is one of the most common specific phobias seen in children, but it can persist well into adulthood if left unaddressed.

If you had to distill nyctophobia to its core: it is an intense, irrational, and persistent fear of darkness or night that goes far beyond normal caution, causes real physical and emotional distress, and can significantly disrupt a person's daily life — but it is a recognized condition that responds well to proper psychological treatment.
11201: A nymph is a word with more than one meaning, and all of its meanings are quite distinct from each other. The most important and widely known meaning comes from ancient mythology, but the word also has a scientific use in biology and a use in fishing.
Meaning 1: A Spirit of Nature (Greek and Roman Mythology)

This is the original, primary, and most well-known meaning of the word.

In ancient Greek and Roman belief, a nymph was a female spirit that lived in and represented a part of nature — such as a river, a tree, a mountain, the sea, or a meadow. Think of nymphs as the living souls of the natural world. The ancient Greeks believed that almost every corner of nature had its own nymph dwelling within it or presiding over it.

Nymphs were imagined as beautiful young women, always feminine, and were considered to be a kind of minor goddess — not as powerful as the great gods like Zeus or Athena, but still supernatural and divine in their own right.

Key things to understand about mythological nymphs:

  • They were tied to a specific place or natural feature. A nymph of a river was that river, in a spiritual sense. If the river dried up, the nymph was believed to die with it. A tree nymph was bound to her tree in the same way.
  • They were very long-lived, but not always immortal. Unlike the major gods, who could never die, most nymphs could eventually perish — just over an extraordinarily long time, or if their home in nature was destroyed.
  • They were attendants and companions to the major gods. Nymphs often served as followers of the goddess Artemis (goddess of the hunt), accompanying her through the forests.
  • They could interact with humans — sometimes lovingly, sometimes playfully, and occasionally dangerously. Many Greek myths involve a hero or a god falling in love with a nymph.

The Different Types of Nymphs

Because nymphs were spirits of specific parts of nature, they were divided into many different groups depending on where they lived. Here are the most important ones:

  • Naiads — Nymphs of freshwater: rivers, streams, springs, brooks, and lakes.
  • Nereids — Nymphs of the sea (specifically the calm Mediterranean Sea). The most famous Nereid is Thetis, the mother of the hero Achilles.
  • Oceanids — Nymphs of the great world ocean that the Greeks believed encircled the entire earth.
  • Dryads — Nymphs of the forests and trees. Sometimes the term Hamadryad is used specifically for a nymph that is bonded to one particular tree and lives only as long as that tree survives.
  • Oreads — Nymphs of mountains and rocky caves. The famous Echo from mythology was an Oread.
  • Limnades — Nymphs of still lakes and marshes.
  • Leimoniades — Nymphs of meadows and flowers.
  • Aurae — Nymphs of breezes and the gentle wind.
  • Napaeae — Nymphs of glens, valleys, and wooded dells.

So when you read the word "nymph" in a mythological or classical literary context, it refers to one of these beautiful, nature-bound female spirits.
Meaning 2: A Beautiful Young Woman (Literary/Poetic Use)

Flowing naturally from its mythological roots, the word "nymph" is also used in poetry, literature, and elevated writing to describe a beautiful, graceful, and youthful woman — the comparison being that she is as lovely as the mythological nymphs were said to be.

This is a figurative, complimentary use of the word. You might encounter it in older poetry, classical plays, or romantic literature. For example, a poet might address a young woman as a nymph to suggest she has an otherworldly, enchanting beauty.

This meaning is less common in everyday modern speech, and when it does appear, it is almost always in artistic or poetic contexts.

This is a completely separate meaning used in science, specifically in the study of insects (entomology).

A nymph is the immature, juvenile stage of certain insects as they grow into adults.

To understand this clearly, you need to know that not all insects grow up in the same way. Some insects — like butterflies and beetles — go through four completely distinct stages: egg → larva (e.g., a caterpillar) → pupa (a cocoon stage) → adult. This is called complete metamorphosis.

Other insects, however, skip that pupal/cocoon stage entirely. They go through only three stages: egg → nymph → adult. This is called incomplete metamorphosis. The young insect that hatches from the egg and gradually grows into an adult — without ever going through a cocoon or dramatically different larval stage — is called a nymph.

Key features of an insect nymph:

  • It looks like a small, miniature version of the adult, not a totally different creature (unlike a caterpillar, which looks nothing like a butterfly).
  • It grows by molting — it sheds its outer skin (called an exoskeleton) several times as it gets bigger. Each stage between molts is called an instar.
  • It usually does not have fully developed wings yet. The wings grow progressively larger with each molt until the nymph becomes a fully winged adult.

Examples of insects that have a nymph stage:

  • Grasshoppers
  • Locusts
  • Dragonflies and damselflies
  • Cockroaches
  • Crickets
  • Mayflies
  • Stink bugs
  • Cicadas

So a baby grasshopper — which looks like a tiny, wingless grasshopper and will gradually grow into a full adult — is called a nymph.
Meaning 4: An Artificial Fishing Fly (Fly Fishing)

This is a more specialized, niche meaning used in the sport of fly fishing.

In fly fishing, fishermen use light, carefully crafted artificial "flies" — fake insects made from feathers, thread, and hooks — to attract and catch fish. A nymph, in this context, is a specific type of artificial fishing fly that is designed to mimic the underwater nymph stage of an aquatic insect (such as a mayfly or dragonfly nymph).

Because fish feed heavily on real insect nymphs underwater, a fishing nymph lure imitates this natural food source and is designed to sink below the water's surface, drifting along the bottom or mid-water where fish feed. This distinguishes it from a "dry fly," which floats on the surface of the water.

If you see the word "nymph" in a fishing, outdoors, or sporting context, this is what it refers to.
How to Know Which Meaning Is Intended

Since the word has multiple meanings, context is your guide:

  • In mythology, history, classical literature, or poetry → it means a female nature spirit (or a beautiful young woman).
  • In biology, zoology, nature documentaries, or science → it means the immature stage of an insect.
  • In fishing, fly-tying, or angling → it means an artificial fly lure.

ContextWhat "nymph" means
Mythology & literatureA female nature spirit; or a beautiful young woman
BiologyA juvenile insect in the stage between egg and adult
Fly fishingAn artificial lure mimicking an aquatic insect nymph
11202: A nymphet is a young girl — typically between about 9 and 14 years old — who is perceived by an older man as being mysteriously, unnervingly attractive or seductive. The key word here is perceived: the word describes how a certain type of man looks at a child, not any actual quality the child possesses.

This word has two distinct but connected meanings. You need both to fully understand it.

1. The Mythological Meaning (older, background sense)

In ancient Greek mythology, nymphs were female nature spirits — divine, ethereally beautiful beings associated with rivers, forests, and mountains. A nymphet originally just meant a young or small nymph. Think of it as the "junior version" of a nymph. This sense carries the ideas of youth, otherworldly beauty, and an enchanting, almost magical quality.

2. The Literary Meaning (dominant modern sense)

This is the meaning that matters most in modern usage, and it comes almost entirely from one source: Vladimir Nabokov's 1955 novel Lolita.

In that novel, the narrator — a deeply disturbed adult man named Humbert Humbert — invents his own private vocabulary to describe his obsession with young girls. He uses the word nymphet to describe a very specific type of child: a girl between roughly 9 and 14 who strikes him as possessing a hidden, uncanny, almost supernatural power of attraction that he believes ordinary little girls do not have.

This is crucial to understand: Humbert does not use the word neutrally. He uses it to convince himself (and tries to convince the reader) that these girls are somehow special, almost supernatural beings — not ordinary children. It is his way of twisting reality to justify his own predatory desires. He is constructing a fantasy.
What Makes This Word Unusual and Important to Understand

The word nymphet is deceptive by design. Here's why:

  • It sounds beautiful and poetic (owing to its mythological roots), which is exactly the effect Nabokov intended — to show how a predator glamorizes and distorts his perception of a child.
  • The beauty of the word masks something deeply sinister: it is the vocabulary of abuse, of an adult projecting desire onto a child who has no such power or intention.
  • The child is not the problem. The "nymphet" is not a real category of human being. It exists only in the mind of the observer. Nabokov was not saying such girls exist; he was showing us how a certain type of dangerous man thinks.

Nabokov, a masterful writer, was criticizing Humbert's worldview, not endorsing it. The novel is a dark, ironic portrait of a criminal mind that uses beautiful language to dress up ugly acts.
How the Word Is Used Today

After Lolita became a globally read classic, the word nymphet entered the broader cultural vocabulary. You may encounter it in:

  • Literary criticism and academic writing, when discussing Lolita or related themes of predation, the male gaze, or the sexualization of children in media and culture.
  • Film and cultural commentary, often when analyzing how certain movies or advertisements have historically portrayed young girls through an adult male gaze.
  • Casual/loose usage (less precise), where some people use it simply to mean an attractive young woman — but this usage strips out the word's critical meaning and is generally considered sloppy or even irresponsible.

A nymphet is a young girl (typically 9–14) who is perceived by a predatory adult man as having a strange, bewitching, otherworldly sexual allure — a perception that exists entirely in the observer's distorted mind, not in the child herself.
Why This Word Matters Beyond a Dictionary Entry

Understanding "nymphet" properly is important because:

  1. You cannot understand Lolita without it — the entire novel is built around this word and the psychology it represents.
  2. It teaches you that language can be weaponized — a beautiful-sounding word can be used to obscure harm.
  3. It appears frequently in serious discussions of child protection, media studies, and feminist criticism, where understanding its precise meaning is essential.

Knowing this word means knowing both what it says on the surface and what it exposes about the mindset that produced it.
11203: An oaf is a person who is clumsy, stupid, or socially awkward — or all three at once. It's almost always used to describe a man or boy. The word paints a picture of someone big, lumbering, and blundering through the world without awareness or grace.

The word captures one or more of these qualities:

1. Physical clumsiness
An oaf moves in a rough, ungainly way. He bumps into things, knocks things over, trips, spills, and generally occupies space like a wrecking ball. His body seems too large or too clumsy for the world around him.

"The oaf tripped over the doorstep and sent the entire tray of food flying."

2. Stupidity or dullness of mind
An oaf doesn't think things through. He's slow to understand, makes careless mistakes, and often fails to grasp what's obvious to everyone else.

"Only an oaf would sign a contract without reading it."

3. Social unawareness or rudeness
An oaf doesn't know — or doesn't care — how to behave properly around people. He says the wrong thing, interrupts, embarrasses others, and generally lacks the social instincts that most people take for granted.

"He spent the whole dinner talking with his mouth full, the oaf."

There's a strong association between the word oaf and large physical size. You'll often hear phrases like "big oaf" or "great lumbering oaf." The image is of a large, heavy, slow-moving man who crashes through situations — physically or socially — without finesse. Think of a bull in a china shop, but in human form.

That said, size is not required. You can call a small, scrawny person an oaf too, if they're clumsy or stupid enough.
Tone: Insult, Mostly — But Sometimes Warm

Oaf is an insult, but it sits on a spectrum:

  • Genuinely offensive: When used in anger or contempt, it's a real put-down. "Get out of my way, you oaf!"
  • Affectionately teasing: Between friends or family, it can be said with warmth or humour, especially when the clumsiness is harmless. "Oh, you broke the cup again? You're such an oaf!" — said with a laugh and a shake of the head.

Context and tone of voice determine which end of the spectrum you're on.
Oaf is a casual, informal word. You'd say it in conversation, use it in a novel, or write it in an informal message. You would not find it in a legal document, a formal report, or academic writing.

• "Don't let that oaf near the china — he'll smash something."
  • "She finally broke up with him. He was a sweet oaf, but he never knew what she needed."
  • "The new guy is a complete oaf — he somehow managed to delete the entire project on his first day."
  • "A great oaf of a man squeezed into the seat next to me on the bus."

FormWordExample
AdjectiveoafishHis oafish behaviour embarrassed everyone.
AdverboafishlyHe oafishly knocked over her drink.
Abstract nounoafishnessHis oafishness was endearing, in a way.
PluraloafsA group of oafs was arguing at the corner.
How It Differs from Similar Words

English has several words for foolish or clumsy people. Here's how oaf is distinct:

  • Fool — emphasises stupidity or foolish decisions, not clumsiness. A fool can be graceful.
  • Clod — similar to oaf, but more specifically about clumsiness or dullness; slightly more old-fashioned.
  • Lout — focuses more on rudeness and bad manners, less on clumsiness or stupidity. A lout is aggressively uncouth.
  • Brute — emphasises physical roughness or violence, often with a cruel edge. A brute is more threatening than an oaf.
  • Dolt — purely about stupidity, with no strong physical clumsiness implied.
  • Buffoon — a foolish, ridiculous person, but often one who makes others laugh (even unintentionally). A buffoon is more comic; an oaf is more irritating.

An oaf is the sweet spot of clumsiness + stupidity + social unawareness, wrapped in a physically large-and-lumbering image. That specific combination is what makes it unique.

An oaf is a clumsy, thick-headed, socially graceless person — usually male, often large — who blunders through situations without awareness or care, and the word is an informal insult that can sometimes be used with mild affection.
11204:
An oasis is a small, fertile area found in the middle of a desert — a place where water exists beneath or on the surface of the ground. Because water is present, plants grow there (most famously, palm trees), animals can survive, and people can rest, drink, and live.

Picture a vast, burning desert — nothing but sand, heat, and dryness for miles. Now imagine suddenly coming across a patch of green trees, grass, and a pool of fresh water right in the middle of that desert. That is an oasis.

The key idea is contrast: the oasis is alive and nourishing, while everything around it is harsh and lifeless. It doesn't just exist — it stands out sharply against its surroundings.

Oases (that's the plural) are not accidents. They form where underground water rises close enough to the surface to feed plant life. They have been historically critical as stopping points for travelers crossing deserts — a place to refill water, rest, and recover before continuing the dangerous journey.

This is where the word truly comes alive in everyday language.

Because a desert oasis gives relief in a harsh, difficult environment, people use "oasis" to describe anything — a place, a moment, a person, or a situation — that provides comfort, calm, or pleasure in the middle of something difficult, stressful, or unpleasant.

The "desert" in the figurative sense doesn't have to be literal. It can be:

  • A stressful job
  • A chaotic city
  • A hard period in life
  • A boring or painful experience

And the "oasis" is whatever breaks that harshness and gives you a breath of relief.

Examples:

  • "The small park in the middle of the busy city was an oasis of calm."
    → The city is loud and hectic (the "desert"); the park is peaceful and restorative (the oasis).
  • "After a brutal week at work, the weekend felt like a true oasis."
    → The exhausting week is the harsh environment; the weekend is the relief.
  • "Her home was an oasis of warmth in an otherwise cold and lonely city."
    → The city feels cold and unfriendly; her home is the safe, welcoming contrast.
  • "The library was an oasis for students during exam season."
    → Exam season is stressful and overwhelming; the quiet library provides relief and focus.

Notice the pattern: there is always something difficult or unpleasant surrounding the oasis, and the oasis is the refuge within it.
The Exact Feeling the Word Carries

"Oasis" is not a neutral word. It carries a feeling of relief, gratitude, and preciousness. When you call something an oasis, you're not just saying it's nice — you're saying it is especially valuable because of how harsh the surrounding situation is. A pool of water is ordinary in a city; in a desert, it is everything. That sense of "this is rare and I deeply need it" is baked into the word.

This is why the word is often used in emotional or dramatic contexts. Calling a place an "oasis" elevates it — it says that without this, things would be much harder to bear.

The most common structure you'll see is:

"an oasis of [something good]"

  • an oasis of peace
  • an oasis of silence
  • an oasis of hope
  • an oasis of normalcy
  • an oasis of beauty

The word after "of" tells you what kind of relief the oasis is providing.

You can also use it directly:

  • "This café is my oasis."
  • "She found an oasis in her friendship with him."
  • "The trip was an oasis."

The plural of oasis is oases (pronounced oh-AY-seez). This is important to know because English learners often mistakenly say "oasises," which is wrong.

  • "The desert has several oases that traders used historically."
  • "These small bookshops are oases for readers in a world of screens."

LiteralA fertile, water-bearing spot in a desert
FigurativeAny source of relief, calm, or pleasure within a difficult or unpleasant situation
Core feelingRare, precious relief that stands out sharply against hardship
PluralOases

The beauty of this word is that its literal and figurative meanings are perfectly aligned — both describe the same essential truth: something life-giving and welcome, surrounded by difficulty. Once you feel that image, you'll never forget what "oasis" means.
11205:
An oath is a serious, formal promise — one that carries much more weight than an everyday promise. What makes an oath different from a regular promise is that when you take an oath, you are calling upon something you consider deeply sacred, holy, or supremely important (such as God, a holy book, your honor, or the law itself) as your witness and guarantor. You are essentially saying: "I swear this is true / I will do this — and I stake something I hold sacred on it."

Because something sacred is invoked, breaking an oath is considered not just a betrayal of another person, but a moral or spiritual violation of the highest order.
The Two Core Types of Oaths

Oaths come in two fundamental forms:

1. A sworn statement of truth — Here, a person swears that something they are saying is true. They are making a solemn declaration of fact.

A witness in a courtroom places their hand on a holy book and takes an oath before testifying. By doing so, they are formally declaring: "What I am about to say is the truth." This is why lying in court after taking such an oath is a serious crime called perjury — you didn't just lie, you broke a sacred promise.

2. A sworn commitment to do something — Here, a person solemnly promises that they will do something, usually a duty or a role they are taking on.

When a new president is inaugurated, they take an oath of office — a formal, public promise to faithfully carry out the duties of their position. When a soldier enlists, they take an oath to defend their country. When a doctor qualifies, they take an oath to uphold the ethics of medicine.

Both types share the same essence: extreme seriousness, public formality, and the invocation of something greater than a casual agreement.
What Makes an Oath Different from a Regular Promise

A regular promise is personal and informal. You make it between yourself and another person. If you break it, you have let someone down.

An oath, however, has these additional layers:

  • Formality: Oaths are almost always performed as a recognized ritual or ceremony, often with specific words, a specific setting, and sometimes witnesses or an audience.
  • A sacred or authoritative witness: You are not just promising to another person — you are swearing before something: God, the law, your nation, your honor. That witness elevates the promise into a binding moral contract.
  • Public weight: Because oaths are usually taken in front of others, breaking one damages not just a relationship but your reputation, integrity, and standing in society.
  • Legal or institutional standing: In many contexts, oaths have legal force. Taking an oath in a courtroom, for example, means the law holds you accountable for what you say.
Common Situations Where Oaths Are Taken

• In a court of law: Witnesses swear to tell the truth before giving testimony.
  • When assuming public office: Presidents, judges, military officers, and other officials swear an oath of office before they begin their duties.
  • In religious or spiritual life: Marriage vows in religious ceremonies are a form of oath. Monks, priests, and nuns take vows (a closely related concept) before God.
  • In medicine: Doctors traditionally take the Hippocratic Oath, pledging to practice medicine ethically and to do no harm.
  • In the military: Soldiers swear an oath of allegiance to their country or constitution.
  • In civic life: Immigrants taking citizenship in a new country often swear an oath of allegiance.
The Second Meaning: A Profane Exclamation

The word oath has a second, entirely different meaning. It can also refer to a swear word or a curse — a profane, irreverent, or offensive exclamation that someone utters, usually in anger, shock, frustration, or pain.

"He stubbed his toe and let out a string of oaths."

This meaning comes from the historical practice of swearing by something sacred (like God's name) in everyday speech as an expression of strong emotion. Over time, such exclamations became what we now call swear words or profanity. When someone "swears" in casual speech (e.g., curses or uses foul language), this is the distant echo of that original sense.

In modern usage, this second meaning is less common in formal writing but appears in literature and older texts.

"To take an oath" — to formally swear or promise something.

"She took an oath of secrecy before joining the organization."

"To swear an oath" — same as above; to make a solemn vow.

"The soldiers swore an oath of allegiance to their country."

"Under oath" — in a legal context, this means you have already sworn to tell the truth and are now legally bound by that promise.

"The witness was under oath when she made that statement."

"On oath" — same as "under oath."

"He declared on oath that he had never met the accused."

"To break an oath" — to fail to keep the promise you solemnly made. This is considered a grave moral failure.

"A knight who breaks his oath of loyalty is considered dishonorable."

"To keep / honor an oath" — to fulfill the promise you made.

"An oath of office" — the formal promise made by someone entering a position of public authority.

"An oath of allegiance" — a solemn promise to be loyal to a nation, ruler, or institution.
The Feeling and Weight of an Oath

The most important thing to understand about an oath is its gravity — the profound seriousness it carries. An oath is not something you give lightly. Societies across history and cultures have treated oaths as one of the most binding things a person can do with their words. In many traditions, swearing falsely (making an oath you know to be untrue or that you have no intention of keeping) is considered a sin, a crime, or both.

This is why phrases like "I swear to God" or "on my honor" or "as God is my witness" carry more emotional force than simply saying "I promise" — they are echoes of the oath tradition, invoking something beyond the self to stand behind one's words.

An oath (noun) is a solemn, formal declaration — either of truth or of commitment — made by invoking something sacred or supremely authoritative as a witness. It is far weightier than a casual promise. It binds you morally, often legally, and sometimes spiritually. Oaths mark some of the most important moments in public life: entering office, giving testimony, serving in the military, or taking on a sacred duty. Secondarily, the word also refers to a profane exclamation or swear word. The single thread connecting all uses is the idea of invoking something greater than yourself with your words — whether in solemn commitment or explosive emotion.
11206:
Oatmeal starts with oats — a type of cereal grain grown as a crop. Raw oat grains in their whole, unprocessed form are not very easy to eat or cook with directly. So they go through processing: they are either ground into a coarse powder, cut into small pieces, or rolled flat. The result of this processing is what we call oatmeal — the dry, processed form of oats that is ready to be used in cooking.

Think of it this way: a wheat grain is processed into flour. Similarly, an oat grain is processed into oatmeal. Oatmeal is oats in a form that humans can conveniently cook and eat.

In its most basic sense, oatmeal is the dry, processed oat product — what you find in a packet or a container in a kitchen. It looks like flat, pale flakes or small, rough grains, depending on the type. It has an off-white to pale tan color.

Not all oatmeal looks the same, because oats can be processed in different ways. There are three main types you will commonly encounter:

Steel-cut oats (also called Irish oatmeal or coarse oatmeal): Here, the whole oat grain is simply chopped into a few rough, small pieces using steel blades — like dicing something with a knife. These are the least processed form. They look like tiny, rough, chunky nuggets. They take the longest to cook (around 20–30 minutes) and have a chewy texture when cooked.

Rolled oats (also called old-fashioned oats): Here, the oat grains are first steamed to soften them, then flattened out using large rollers, producing thin, flat flakes. These are the most common and widely used type. They cook faster than steel-cut oats (around 5 minutes) and have a softer, slightly chewy texture.

Quick oats / Instant oats: These are rolled oats that have been processed even further — rolled thinner and sometimes cut into smaller pieces. They cook in just 1–3 minutes. Instant oats often come in pre-portioned packets with added flavoring (like "apple cinnamon" or "maple brown sugar"). They are the softest and least chewy when cooked.

Ground oatmeal / oat flour: When oats are ground very finely into a powder, the result is sometimes called oatmeal (especially in older British usage) or, more commonly today, oat flour. This form is used in baking.

All of these — the chunky steel-cut pieces, the flat rolled flakes, the finely ground powder — are different forms of oatmeal. The word covers all of them when used in this sense.

The second major meaning of oatmeal is the hot, cooked food made by boiling the dry oatmeal (usually rolled oats or steel-cut oats) in water or milk. When heat is applied, the oats absorb the liquid and soften into a thick, creamy, slightly sticky mixture — warm, soft, and filling. This cooked dish is also called oatmeal.

This usage is especially common in American English. If an American says, "I had oatmeal for breakfast," they almost certainly mean the cooked, warm dish — not the dry flakes.

In British English, this same cooked dish is more typically called porridge, not oatmeal. So the word choice can differ by region, but the dish is the same.

Oatmeal as a cooked dish is one of the most common breakfast foods in many parts of the world. It can be eaten plain or topped with things like fruit, nuts, honey, sugar, cinnamon, milk, butter, or jam. It is known for being filling and nutritious.

A popular modern variation is overnight oats — rolled oats soaked in milk or yogurt overnight in the refrigerator without any cooking. They soften on their own and are eaten cold. Despite not being cooked, this is still considered a form of oatmeal.

"Oatmeal" is also used as a color name. It refers to a pale, warm, creamy off-white or light beige — the natural color of uncooked rolled oats or the cooked dish. It is softer and warmer than pure white, with a slight yellowish or tan tint.

You will hear this word used as a color in fashion and clothing ("an oatmeal-colored sweater," "oatmeal linen trousers"), interior design ("oatmeal walls," "an oatmeal carpet"), and product descriptions. It is a neutral, understated, natural-looking color.

Oatmeal bath / colloidal oatmeal: Finely ground oatmeal, when mixed into bathwater, has a soothing effect on irritated or itchy skin (such as from eczema, sunburn, or rashes). This is a well-known home remedy and is also used in skin-care products. Here, the word "oatmeal" still refers to the ground grain, but it is being used for skin care rather than eating.

Oatmeal cookies: A very popular type of cookie made using rolled oats as a key ingredient. The oats give the cookie a slightly chewy, hearty texture. An "oatmeal raisin cookie" (with oats and raisins) is a classic variety.

Oatmeal stout: A type of dark beer brewed with oatmeal added during the process, giving it a smooth, slightly creamy texture.

To make things concrete, here are examples of the word being used in natural, everyday speech:

  • "I poured the oatmeal into the bowl and added milk." → Here, "oatmeal" refers to dry rolled oats (the ingredient).
  • "She made a bowl of oatmeal every morning." → Here, "oatmeal" refers to the hot, cooked dish.
  • "The walls were painted a soft oatmeal." → Here, "oatmeal" is used as a color.
  • "Doctors sometimes recommend an oatmeal bath for children with chickenpox." → Here, it refers to finely ground oatmeal used for skin relief.
  • "Do you prefer steel-cut oatmeal or instant?" → Here, "oatmeal" refers to the type of dry oat product.

The word oatmeal (noun) has three overlapping uses:

  1. The dry ingredient — oats that have been ground, cut, or rolled for cooking. This includes steel-cut oats, rolled oats, and instant oats.
  2. The cooked dish — the warm, thick porridge made by cooking those oats in water or milk. (Especially used this way in American English.)
  3. The color — a warm, pale, creamy off-white, like the natural color of oats.

In everyday life, when someone says "oatmeal," they most often mean either the dry oat product in a container or the hot breakfast dish made from it. The color meaning appears mainly in design and fashion. All uses share a connection to the appearance or substance of the oat grain.
11207:
Obduracy is the quality of being stubbornly, almost unmoveably resistant — either to changing your mind, or to feeling guilt and compassion — even when every reason in the world is telling you that you should.

Think of a stone wall. You can push it, reason with it, plead with it, cry in front of it — it doesn't move. Doesn't flinch. Doesn't care. That stone-wall quality in a person is obduracy.
The Two Sides of Its Meaning

This word carries two closely related but distinct shades of meaning, and understanding both is key.

Side 1 — Stubbornly refusing to change your position

This is the more common meaning. A person showing obduracy will not budge from their stance, decision, or course of action, no matter how strong the argument against it, how much pressure is applied, or how obvious it is that they are wrong. This goes beyond normal stubbornness. It is a deep, settled, almost fortress-like refusal to yield.

The management's obduracy during the negotiations left the workers no choice but to go on strike.

Here, the management simply will not move. Not "we need more time to think" — but a flat, entrenched refusal.

Side 2 — Hardness of heart; refusing to feel remorse

This is the moral dimension of the word. It describes a person who has done something wrong but feels no guilt, no regret, and no desire to change or make amends. Their heart is hardened. Appeals to conscience bounce right off them.

Even after seeing the devastation his policies had caused, the general's obduracy was chilling — he expressed no regret whatsoever.

This sense of the word has historically appeared often in moral and religious writing, where a person who refuses to repent or feel sorry for their sins is said to show obduracy.
The Key Feeling the Word Carries

Obduracy is always negative. This is important.

The word is never used to describe someone in a flattering way. When you call someone's behaviour "obduracy," you are passing a judgment — you are saying that their refusal to change or feel something is unreasonable, unjustified, and probably harmful. There is a slight air of cold, even cruel, indifference about the word.

This is what separates it from words like determination or conviction, which describe admirable qualities of standing firm. Obduracy implies the person should soften, should listen, should feel something — but they simply won't. There is something almost inhuman about it.
How It Differs From Similar Words

Several words feel close to obduracy, but each has a slightly different flavour:

Stubbornness — This is the everyday, casual version. A child being stubborn about eating vegetables is not being obdurate. Stubbornness can sometimes be seen as endearing or even useful. Obduracy is stronger, more entrenched, and always carries a negative judgment.

Obstinacy — Very close to obduracy, but obstinacy is mainly about refusing to change your mind or opinion. Obduracy goes further — it also captures that hardness of heart, that lack of moral feeling. Obduracy is obstinacy with a colder, more morally charged edge.

Inflexibility — This is neutral and broad. A schedule can be "inflexible." A rule can be "inflexible." Obduracy is personal, human, and morally loaded. It always implies a kind of blame.

Intransigence — This is the closest near-synonym. Both words describe an unwillingness to compromise or change position. However, intransigence tends to be used purely in the context of disputes, negotiations, or political positions. Obduracy covers that and the moral/emotional dimension of hardheartedness.

• It is not the same as being slow to decide. An obdurate person may decide quickly — they just won't be moved once they have.
  • It is not calm confidence in the face of opposition. A confident, principled person changes their mind when given good reason — an obdurate person doesn't.
  • It is not caution or careful resistance. Obduracy is not thoughtful — it is a kind of sealed-off, unchallengeable resistance.
Who or What Can Show Obduracy

Usually a person — a leader, a parent, an official, a criminal, a negotiator.

But it is also commonly applied to groups, governments, or institutions:

The regime's obduracy in the face of international pressure was extraordinary.

It is rarely used to describe abstract things. It is almost always attached to something with a will — a being that could choose to change, but simply refuses to.
Example Sentences Showing It in Full Use

1. "His obduracy was legendary — no one in thirty years of working with him had ever seen him reverse a decision."

(He never changes his mind. Period.)

  1. "The obduracy of the convicted man, who showed no remorse even at sentencing, disturbed everyone in the courtroom."

(He felt nothing. No guilt. No regret.)

  1. "Faced with the obduracy of the local council, the residents finally gave up trying to have the law changed."

(The council simply would not move, no matter what.)

  1. "What made him dangerous was not his cruelty alone, but his obduracy — the complete impossibility of reaching him through reason or conscience."

(Both meanings working together — unreachable by logic AND unreachable by moral feeling.)
The One Mental Image to Remember It By

If you ever forget what this word means, picture a judge sitting completely still, arms folded, face like stone, while everyone around them weeps, argues, and pleads — and the judge simply stares ahead, unmoved, unchanging, feeling nothing.

That is obduracy. The stone that will not be softened.
11208: If someone is obdurate, they are stubbornly and completely unwilling to change their mind, attitude, or behavior — even when faced with very good reasons, emotional appeals, or moral arguments to do so. Think of their mind as a wall: you can knock on it, reason with it, beg it, cry in front of it — and it simply will not budge.
The heart of the word — and what makes it special

Many words describe stubbornness, but "obdurate" is a cut above. It doesn't just mean someone is stubborn in a casual, ordinary way. It carries a sense of hardness of heart. An obdurate person isn't simply forgetting to change — they are consciously, actively refusing to be moved, and often in situations where most reasonable or compassionate people would be moved. This is why the word has a strong moral weight to it. It implies a kind of coldness or indifference to persuasion, emotion, or conscience.
Two closely related shades of meaning

The word works in two situations, both rooted in the same core idea of being unmovable:

The first is intellectual stubbornness — refusing to change a decision, opinion, or course of action even when others present compelling arguments or beg you to reconsider. For example, a landlord who refuses to lower rent despite knowing his tenants are struggling financially, no matter how much they plead, is being obdurate.

The second shade is moral hardness or lack of remorse — being so hardened that you feel no guilt, regret, or shame for something you have done wrong. For example, a criminal who sits in a courtroom and shows zero remorse, completely untouched by the gravity of their crime, could be described as obdurate. This second shade was historically more common, but today both senses are used.

What unites both shades is the image of someone who has heard everything there is to hear — the arguments, the tears, the moral case — and has remained completely, almost unnaturally, unmoved.

"Obdurate" is a formal word. You will encounter it more in writing — literary fiction, newspapers, legal and political commentary, formal speeches — than in everyday conversation. Using it signals that you are speaking with precision and weight. It is not the kind of word you'd use lightly to describe someone who simply won't share the TV remote.
How it compares to similar words

Understanding a word also means knowing how it differs from its neighbors.

Stubborn is the most everyday word and the most neutral of the group. A stubborn child refusing to eat vegetables is mildly annoying, but we don't necessarily think of them as morally flawed.

Obstinate is a step stronger than stubborn. It suggests persistence in refusing, often unreasonably, and carries a more negative tone.

Obdurate is the strongest and most formal of the three. It implies not just that someone refuses to budge, but that they are doing so with a kind of hardened indifference — often to emotional or moral pressure specifically. An obdurate person isn't just being difficult; they are being unyielding in a way that feels cold or even callous.

Adamant means firmly insisting on something and can sometimes be used in a neutral or even admirable sense ("she was adamant about protecting the children"). Obdurate almost never carries a positive sense.

Intransigent means refusing to compromise, especially in political or ideological contexts. It is close to obdurate but tends to be used more in the context of negotiations and disputes between groups or institutions.

"Despite the tears of his own family, the dictator remained obdurate, refusing to release the prisoners." — Here, his coldness in the face of emotional family appeals makes him obdurate.

"The committee was obdurate in its decision to close the school, brushing aside every petition and protest from the community." — Here, they are stubbornly unmoved by public pressure.

"The convicted man stood before the judge, obdurate and unrepentant, as if he saw nothing wrong with what he had done." — Here, the moral hardness and lack of remorse is the focus.

"She made every argument she could think of, but he was obdurate — his mind had been made up long before she walked into the room." — Here, the sense of an almost predetermined refusal to be persuaded comes through.
A mental image to make it stick

Picture a boulder in the middle of a river. The water — representing your arguments, your tears, your appeals to reason and conscience — flows around it, crashes against it, begs it to move. The boulder does not shift. It does not crack. It sits there, cold and hard and completely indifferent. That boulder is obdurate. Now put a human face on that boulder, and you have the word in action.
Obdurate means stubbornly hardened against change, persuasion, or remorse — unmoved by arguments, emotions, or moral pressure that would soften most people.
11209:
Obedience is the act of following instructions, rules, commands, or laws given by someone or something with authority over you — and doing so willingly, consistently, and without resistance.

When someone shows obedience, they are essentially saying through their actions: "You have the right to tell me what to do, and I will do it."

Three things are always present in obedience:

  1. A source of authority — a person, institution, law, or belief system that issues a command or sets a rule. (A parent, a government, a religion, a commanding officer, a teacher.)
  2. A person who receives that command — the one who is expected to follow.
  3. The act of following — actually doing what was asked or required.

If any one of these is missing, what you have is not obedience. For example, if you do something no one asked you to do, that is initiative, not obedience. If you are forced against your will with no choice at all, that is closer to coercion, not obedience in the full sense.
The Key Idea: Compliance + Submission to Authority

Obedience is not just doing the right thing — it is specifically doing what you were told to do because you were told to do it, by someone whose authority you recognize or accept (even if reluctantly).

This is what separates obedience from similar-looking behavior:

  • A soldier who follows orders because a general commanded it → obedience
  • A person who stops at a red light because they genuinely believe it keeps people safe → good judgment or conscience, not obedience per se
  • A child who is physically dragged to school → force, not obedience

The element of recognition of authority is what makes obedience what it is.

Obedience is not a simple on/off switch. It exists on a spectrum:

Immediate obedience — Following a command right away, without delay.

Reluctant obedience — Doing what you are told, but unhappily, slowly, or with complaint. It is still obedience, but of a weaker or poorer quality.

Blind obedience — Following instructions without questioning them at all, even when they might be wrong or harmful. This is often seen as dangerous.

Conditional obedience — Obeying, but only up to a certain point. ("I will follow this rule, but not if it asks me to harm someone.")

Partial obedience — Doing only part of what was asked. This is sometimes considered disobedience, since true obedience typically means completing the full task as intended.

Obedience shows up in nearly every area of human life:

In family life: A child's obedience to parents is one of the earliest forms of obedience humans experience. Parents set rules — bedtime, diet, behavior — and a child who follows them is showing obedience. This is considered important for a child's safety and development, because children often cannot fully judge consequences themselves.

In religion: Many religions place great value on obedience — to God, to religious texts, or to spiritual leaders. In this context, obedience is often seen as a virtue, a sign of humility, faith, and trust. A monk who follows the rules of a monastery, a believer who follows divine commandments — these are forms of religious obedience.

In the military: Obedience is absolutely central to how armies function. Soldiers are expected to follow orders from superior officers quickly and without questioning them on the battlefield. The entire structure of military power depends on this chain of obedience.

In civil society: Citizens are expected to show obedience to laws — to pay taxes, follow traffic rules, respect court orders. This is sometimes called civic obedience or law-abidingness.

In the workplace: Employees show obedience when they follow policies, carry out instructions from managers, and work within the rules set by an organization.

With animals: The word is also used for animals trained to follow commands — an "obedient dog" is one that sits, stays, and comes when called.

These words are close neighbors of obedience, but each has a slightly different shade of meaning:

Compliance — Following rules or requests, often because you are required to, sometimes out of social pressure rather than genuine respect for authority. It is a bit more neutral and less personal than obedience. You can comply with a policy without really accepting the authority behind it.

Submission — This carries a stronger sense of yielding, of surrendering one's own will entirely to another. Obedience can be dignified and willing; submission often suggests a deeper, sometimes involuntary giving-up of one's own power.

Deference — Respectfully going along with someone else's judgment or wishes, not because they are commanding you, but because you respect them. ("I deferred to her expertise.")

Discipline — Closely related, but discipline refers more to the training or self-control that makes obedience possible, while obedience is the actual behavior that results.

Conformity — Going along with group norms or expectations, often socially driven. Conformity is about matching a group; obedience is about responding to authority.

Obedience is considered a virtue in many traditions and systems because:

  • It allows groups, organizations, and societies to function in an orderly way.
  • It protects people from harm when authority figures have more knowledge or experience.
  • It is seen as a sign of humility — setting aside your own ego or desires for something larger.
  • It builds trust between people at different levels of a relationship (parent-child, teacher-student, commander-soldier).
  • It enables coordination: when everyone follows the same rules, things work.
When Obedience Is Questioned or Criticized

Obedience is not always good. It becomes deeply problematic when:

  • The authority issuing commands is unjust, corrupt, or evil.
  • The command requires you to harm yourself or others.
  • It shuts down your own moral conscience entirely.

The philosopher Hannah Arendt famously described how ordinary people committed terrible acts during the Holocaust largely through blind obedience — simply following orders without moral reflection. This gave rise to the phrase "just following orders," now used to describe the failure of blind obedience.

This is why many thinkers distinguish between obedience and conscience — the idea that there are some commands that should never be obeyed, regardless of who gives them.
Obedience is the willing compliance with the commands, rules, or authority of another — characterized by the recognition of that authority and the consistent act of doing what is required.

Think of obedience as a bridge between authority and action. Someone in authority speaks; the obedient person listens and acts accordingly. It is not simply doing good things — it is specifically doing what you were told to do, by someone you accept as having the right to tell you. It can be a virtue (in a just system, with good authority) or a danger (when it replaces moral thinking entirely). It is one of the most fundamental forces shaping how families, religions, armies, governments, and societies hold together.
11210:
Imagine you are standing before a king. You lower your head, bend your body into a deep bow, and hold it there for a moment. That physical gesture — the bow — is an act of obeisance. It is something you do with your body to show a person (or thing) that you consider them far above you, that you deeply respect and submit to their authority or greatness.

Obeisance means a gesture of deep respect, submission, or homage directed toward someone or something of higher power or importance.

The word carries two senses that are brothers — one physical, one abstract.

1. The Physical Sense (a gesture)

This is the original and most literal meaning. Obeisance is a bodily act performed in front of someone to show reverence and submission. It is most classically a bow, a curtsy, or a full prostration (lying face-down on the ground). The key is that your body is physically lowering itself in the presence of another, which symbolises that you place them above you.

The knight dropped to one knee and made a slow obeisance before the queen.

The priests performed their obeisances at the altar before the ceremony began.

Notice that you do not just casually nod at someone as obeisance — it is a deliberate, formal, deep gesture. It carries weight and intention.

2. The Abstract Sense (an attitude of deference)

Over time, the word expanded beyond just the physical act. Obeisance can also mean the attitude or spirit of deep respect and submission itself — even when no bowing is physically happening. In this sense, it describes the way someone behaves toward a powerful person, idea, institution, or tradition, as though symbolically bowing before it.

The entire government paid obeisance to the old president's wishes, never daring to challenge him.

She refused to make obeisance to popular opinion and stuck firmly to her own views.

Here, nobody is physically bowing. But the spirit is the same — treating something as so powerful or important that you subordinate yourself before it.
The Three Things That Are Always Present

No matter which sense you use, three elements are always baked into the word:

Hierarchy — There is always a "higher" and a "lower." You show obeisance upward, never to an equal or to someone below you.

Submission — It is not just admiration. It carries a flavour of yielding, of placing yourself below the other.

Deliberateness — Obeisance is always a conscious act. It is performed on purpose, not accidental. You make or pay or do obeisance — it is something actively carried out.

Obeisance almost always appears in a small set of fixed phrases:

  • "make obeisance" — the most common phrasing, meaning to perform the gesture or act of submission.
  • "pay obeisance" — very similar; you pay obeisance the way you pay tribute, as an offering of respect.
  • "do obeisance" — slightly older-sounding, but means the same thing.

He bowed his head and made obeisance to the gods.
The citizens were expected to pay obeisance to the emperor during public processions.
The Register and Tone of the Word

This is important for a learner: obeisance is a formal, somewhat literary word. You will not hear it in everyday casual conversation. It appears in:

  • Literature and fiction, especially historical novels, fantasy, or anything with kings, emperors, or religious ceremonies.
  • Formal writing about politics, history, or religion.
  • Critical or ironic commentary, where a writer sarcastically accuses someone of bowing down to a powerful person or idea.

If you use it in speech, it signals that you are being deliberately elevated and formal in your expression.
How It Differs from Similar Words

These words are related but not identical:

Respect is broad and everyday. You can respect a friend, a teacher, a parent. Obeisance is narrower — it suggests a much bigger power gap and a formal, visible act of submission.

Reverence focuses on deep admiration and awe, often with a sacred or spiritual flavour. Obeisance focuses more on the subordination aspect — placing yourself below another.

Homage is very close to obeisance, but homage can also be something positive you offer freely (as in, "paying homage to a great artist"). Obeisance carries a slightly stronger sense of submission — of bowing down, not just honouring.

Deference is the abstract attitude of yielding to another's authority. Obeisance can carry this abstract meaning too, but it always has that physical, gesture-like quality lurking even in its abstract uses.

Think of obeisance as a word that captures the full picture of what happens when someone consciously places themselves below another — whether through a literal bow of the body, or through an attitude of complete submission and deference in behaviour. It is always formal, always intentional, always directed upward toward power, authority, or importance. The word carries a certain gravitas — even a theatrical quality — which is why it lives more in books and formal writing than in everyday speech.
11211: An obelisk is a tall, narrow, four-sided stone pillar that slowly gets thinner as it rises, and ends at the very top in a small pyramid shape. Think of it like a very tall, sharp pencil made of stone — wide at the base, narrow at the top, with all four sides gently sloping inward, and a tiny pointed pyramid sitting at the tip.

Every obelisk has a few defining features that make it instantly recognizable:

  • Four flat sides — each side is a flat, rectangular face
  • Tapered shape — it is widest at the bottom and gets gradually narrower going up
  • A pyramidal tip — the very top ends in a small pyramid shape; this pointed cap is called a pyramidion
  • Massive size — obelisks are typically very tall, often standing anywhere from 10 to over 30 meters high (roughly 30 to 100 feet)
  • Made from a single stone — traditionally, a true obelisk is carved out of one single, massive piece of rock (usually granite), which makes the engineering feat of building one all the more remarkable

Obelisks were invented and perfected by the ancient Egyptians, thousands of years ago. They were not just decorative objects — they held deep religious meaning. The Egyptians connected obelisks to the sun, and the shining pyramidion at the top was meant to catch the first rays of sunlight each morning, symbolizing the power of their sun god.

Obelisks were typically placed in pairs at the entrances of temples, standing like tall guardians on either side of the gateway. Their surfaces were often carved and inscribed with hieroglyphs — the picture-based writing system of ancient Egypt — recording the names of pharaohs and praising the gods.

Over the centuries, obelisks were taken out of Egypt by various empires — the Romans were especially fond of them — and transported to cities across the world. This is why today you can find ancient Egyptian obelisks standing in unexpected places far from Egypt.

Some of the most famous ones include:

  • Cleopatra's Needles — a pair of ancient Egyptian obelisks; one now stands in New York City's Central Park, and the other stands on the Embankment in London
  • The Lateran Obelisk in Rome — the tallest standing ancient obelisk in the world
  • The obelisk in St. Peter's Square, Vatican City

Many countries and cities have also built their own obelisks over the centuries, inspired by the Egyptian originals. Perhaps the most famous modern example is the Washington Monument in Washington, D.C. — while it is not an ancient Egyptian obelisk, it is built in the exact same shape and is considered an obelisk.

In everyday language, when someone says "obelisk," they almost always mean one of two things:

  1. An ancient Egyptian monument — a genuine carved stone pillar from ancient Egypt, or one inspired by that tradition
  2. Any tall, tapering, four-sided pillar built in that classic shape — even if it is modern and made of different materials

You might hear it used like this:

  • "The ancient obelisk towered over the entrance to the temple."
  • "The city erected an obelisk in the town square to honor its fallen soldiers."
  • "The Washington Monument is essentially a giant obelisk."

In a completely different context — the world of printing and writing — the word "obelisk" also refers to a typographical symbol: †. This small dagger-shaped symbol (also called a "dagger") is used in books and documents to mark a footnote or to indicate that a person is deceased. However, this meaning is far less common in everyday speech. When most people say "obelisk," they mean the stone pillar.
The core idea, in one sentence

An obelisk is a tall, four-sided stone pillar, narrowing upward and ending in a pyramid-shaped tip — a shape invented by ancient Egyptians as a religious monument and later adopted worldwide as a symbol of grandeur, commemoration, and architectural elegance.
11212:
Obese describes a person who has accumulated so much excess body fat that it poses a serious risk to their health. This is not simply a matter of looking "big" or carrying a few extra pounds. The word specifically signals that the amount of body fat has crossed a medical threshold — a point where the body is under real, measurable physical strain and where the risk of dangerous diseases rises significantly.

Think of it on a spectrum: a person can be slim, then average, then slightly overweight, and then — at a clearly more serious level — obese. It is not a vague or subjective word. It has a precise clinical definition.

Doctors measure obesity using a tool called the Body Mass Index (BMI), which is a number calculated from a person's height and weight. According to standard medical guidelines:

  • A BMI of 18.5–24.9 is considered normal/healthy.
  • A BMI of 25–29.9 is considered overweight (excess weight, but not yet at the obese level).
  • A BMI of 30 or higher is considered obese.

So, for example, a person who is 5 feet 9 inches (175 cm) tall and weighs around 203 pounds (92 kg) or more would have a BMI of 30, placing them in the "obese" category.

Doctors also recognize different levels of severity within obesity itself:

  • Class I obesity — BMI of 30 to 34.9 (the entry level)
  • Class II obesity — BMI of 35 to 39.9 (more serious)
  • Class III obesity (sometimes called severe or morbid obesity) — BMI of 40 or higher (the most dangerous level)
What Makes It Different From Just "Fat" or "Overweight"

These three words — fat, overweight, and obese — are often used carelessly, so it is worth understanding exactly how they differ.

Fat is a general, informal, everyday word. It simply means having a noticeable amount of body fat. It carries no specific medical measurement behind it. It can also be used as a rude or offensive word when directed at a person, even though it doesn't have to be.

Overweight means a person's weight is above the normal healthy range, but has not yet reached the obese threshold. It is a step above normal — a warning sign — but not yet at the level of serious health danger.

Obese is a formal, clinical, medical word. It means the person has gone beyond overweight and has entered a range where health is genuinely and measurably at risk. The key difference is severity and precision. A doctor calling a patient "obese" is not making a casual comment — they are making a specific clinical judgment based on measurable data.
The Health Consequences That Give the Word Its Weight

The reason "obese" exists as a special, separate medical category is because the health consequences at this level are well-documented and serious. Being obese is strongly linked to:

  • Type 2 diabetes (the body struggles to manage blood sugar)
  • Heart disease and stroke (the heart has to work much harder)
  • High blood pressure (the cardiovascular system is under extra strain)
  • Sleep apnea (breathing repeatedly stops during sleep)
  • Joint damage, especially in the knees and hips (excess weight crushes joints)
  • Certain cancers (including colon, breast, and liver cancer)
  • Mental health difficulties, including depression and anxiety

This is why doctors treat obesity as a medical condition requiring attention and care — not just a cosmetic or lifestyle matter.
The Tone and Register of the Word

"Obese" is a formal, clinical, and neutral word in its intent. It belongs to the language of medicine, science, public health, and academic research. You will hear it from doctors, read it in health reports, and see it in government statistics. In those contexts, it is simply a precise, factual descriptor — no different from "diabetic" or "anemic."

However, in everyday social conversation, calling someone "obese" to their face — rather than in a clinical discussion — can feel cold, blunt, or even hurtful, because the word carries weight (in every sense). Many people are sensitive about their body size, and the word, while medically accurate, can land as harsh in informal settings. This does not make the word wrong or bad — it simply means that context matters. A doctor using it in a consultation is appropriate. A stranger using it as a comment is unkind.
How to Use It in a Sentence

Here are clear, natural examples:

  • "The patient was classified as obese based on his BMI of 33."
  • "The study found that obese adults are twice as likely to develop Type 2 diabetes."
  • "She was told by her doctor that, while not obese, she was overweight and should watch her diet."
  • "Public health campaigns have focused on reducing the number of obese children in the country."
  • "He had been obese most of his adult life, but after lifestyle changes, he lost enough weight to fall into the overweight category."

Since "obese" is the adjective, it is useful to know its family:

  • Obesity (noun) — the condition or state of being obese. "Obesity is a growing public health crisis."
  • Obese (adjective) — the describing word applied to a person. "She is obese."
  • Obesely (adverb) — very rarely used; in practice, you will almost never encounter this form.

The noun form "obesity" is actually used just as often as the adjective in real-world text, especially in news and health writing.

Obese is a formal medical adjective describing a person whose body fat has accumulated to a level — specifically, a BMI of 30 or above — that is measurably dangerous to their health and significantly raises their risk of serious diseases.
11213:
To obfuscate something means to make it deliberately unclear, confusing, or difficult to understand — usually to hide the truth or avoid giving a straight answer.

Think of it this way: imagine someone asking you a direct question, and instead of answering honestly, you respond with a long, tangled, roundabout answer full of vague words and unnecessary complexity — so much so that the other person walks away more confused than before. That is obfuscating.

The most important thing to understand about this word is that it almost always implies intent. When someone obfuscates, they are usually doing it on purpose. It is not just accidental confusion. There is a deliberate effort to cloud the truth, hide information, or make something simple seem complicated so that people can't see what's really going on.

The tone and feeling of the word. Obfuscate carries a strongly negative connotation. When you say someone is obfuscating, you are essentially accusing them of being dishonest, evasive, or manipulative — even if they never technically told a lie. It's a more sophisticated form of deception because the person is not making a false statement; they're just burying the truth under so much fog that it becomes invisible.
Where you'll see this word used in real life:

In politics: This is perhaps the most common place. A politician who is asked "Did you raise taxes?" might respond with a ten-minute speech about economic frameworks, historical precedents, and fiscal responsibility — without ever saying yes or no. That is textbook obfuscation. Journalists often accuse politicians of obfuscating when they dodge direct questions during interviews or debates.

In legal and corporate language: Long contracts and terms-of-service documents often obfuscate what a company is actually allowed to do with your data or money. The information is technically there, but it's buried in so much dense, complex language that the average person can't understand it. The complexity itself is the tool of obfuscation.

In academia and writing: Some writers obfuscate by using unnecessarily complicated jargon or abstract language when simpler words would do just fine. The result is writing that sounds impressive but communicates very little. A sentence like "The ontological underpinnings of relational epistemology necessitate a re-evaluation of subjective frameworks" might just be a very obfuscated way of saying "How we know things depends on our relationships."

In technology: Programmers sometimes deliberately obfuscate their source code — scrambling the structure and variable names so that the code still works but becomes nearly impossible for outsiders to read or copy. This is actually called "code obfuscation" and is a real technical practice.

In everyday life: Obfuscation happens in ordinary conversations too. Someone who is guilty of something might give a confusing, overly detailed account of their day to hide a simple fact. A company might bury a price increase inside a long announcement about "exciting changes." A person might use technical terms to make a basic mistake sound less obvious.
Example sentences to see it in action:

"The manager obfuscated the real reason for the layoffs by talking endlessly about market conditions and strategic realignment."

"His answer was so full of jargon that it only served to obfuscate the issue further."

"The report was deliberately written to obfuscate the company's environmental violations."

"She felt he was obfuscating, giving her every detail except the one she actually needed."

How it differs from similar words. Words like confuse, obscure, conceal, and mislead are all related, but obfuscate has a specific character of its own.

Confuse is more neutral and can be accidental — you might confuse someone without meaning to. But to obfuscate is almost always a deliberate act.

Obscure means to make something unclear or hard to see, and it can be used without implying intent. Fog obscures the road — the fog isn't trying to deceive anyone. But obfuscate nearly always implies a deliberate agent doing the obscuring.

Conceal means to simply hide something outright. Obfuscation is more subtle — the information may technically be present, but it's hidden within complexity, vagueness, or confusion, rather than being removed entirely.

Mislead means to point someone in the wrong direction, often by giving false information. Obfuscation doesn't necessarily involve false information — it works through confusion and overcomplication instead of outright falsehood. This is what makes it particularly sneaky.

The opposite of obfuscate. To do the opposite is to clarify, illuminate, simplify, or elucidate — to make something clear, transparent, and easy to understand.

The one-sentence test to know if you've truly understood this word: If someone is making something needlessly complicated, vague, or confusing — especially to hide the truth or avoid accountability — they are obfuscating. The fog they are creating is the tool, and confusion is the goal.
11214:
Obfuscation means the act of making something unclear, confusing, or difficult to understand. It refers to any process — whether done on purpose or by accident — that muddies, hides, or clouds something that could otherwise be straightforward.

Think of it this way: imagine you ask someone a simple yes-or-no question, and instead of answering, they respond with five minutes of complicated, roundabout, jargon-filled speech that leaves you more confused than before. That is obfuscation at work.
The two faces of obfuscation — deliberate vs. accidental

Obfuscation can happen in two ways, and understanding this distinction is key.

The first is deliberate obfuscation. This is when someone intentionally makes something hard to understand in order to deceive, hide the truth, protect a secret, or avoid accountability. A politician who is caught in a scandal and responds to every question with vague, tangled non-answers is deliberately using obfuscation as a tool of self-defense. A company that buries an important fee inside twelve pages of dense legal fine print is using obfuscation to stop you from noticing what you are agreeing to. In this deliberate sense, obfuscation is essentially a strategy of controlled confusion — the person doing it knows the truth perfectly well, but has chosen to wrap it in fog so that others cannot see it clearly.

The second is accidental obfuscation. This happens when someone makes something confusing not out of bad intent, but because of poor communication skills, excessive use of jargon, or simply not thinking about what the audience needs. A scientist who explains a simple concept using nothing but highly technical terms to a general audience is accidentally causing obfuscation. The intent may be perfectly honest, but the result is the same — confusion and a lack of understanding.

In everyday usage, the word leans more toward the deliberate kind, so when you see or hear "obfuscation," there is usually a subtle implication of intent behind it.
Where you will encounter this word

In politics and public life, obfuscation is extremely common. Politicians, press secretaries, and public relations professionals are often accused of it when they deflect questions, speak in circles, or use carefully chosen language designed to mean as little as possible while sounding like it means a lot. Phrases like "we remain committed to exploring all available strategic frameworks" instead of a direct answer are classic examples of political obfuscation.

In law and business, obfuscation appears in overly complicated contracts, terms of service, and legal documents that are technically readable but practically incomprehensible to ordinary people. The goal, deliberate or not, is the same: a reader who cannot understand what they are agreeing to is a reader who cannot push back on it.

In technology and computing, obfuscation has a specific and well-known meaning. Code obfuscation refers to the practice of deliberately rewriting software code in a way that makes it very difficult for others to read, understand, or copy — while still making sure it works perfectly. Developers sometimes do this to protect their intellectual property. Malicious hackers also use it to hide harmful code so that security tools cannot detect it easily.
