It is a force — felt internally, imposed externally, or both — that pulls you toward a specific action or behaviour, and away from ignoring it.

Think of it this way: when you have an obligation, you do not have a completely free choice. Something — a rule, a promise, a relationship, a law, a moral principle — has already decided for you that a certain action is expected, and that failing to act will have consequences (emotional, social, legal, or otherwise).

Obligations do not arise out of thin air. They are created by something. Here are the main sources:

1. Agreements and Promises
When you agree to do something — whether you sign a contract, make a verbal promise, or shake hands on a deal — you create an obligation. If you tell your friend, "I will help you move this Saturday," you now have an obligation to show up. Breaking it is considered wrong because you gave your word.

2. Laws and Rules
Governments, institutions, and organisations impose formal obligations. Paying taxes is a legal obligation. Following traffic laws is a legal obligation. A student has an obligation to follow school rules. These obligations exist whether you like them or not, because a formal authority demands them.

3. Moral and Ethical Principles
Some obligations come not from any written rule but from a widely shared sense of right and wrong. If you witness a child drowning in a shallow pond and you can save them at no real risk to yourself, most people would say you have a moral obligation to help — even if no law forces you to. These obligations are felt from the inside, from conscience and values.

4. Roles and Relationships
When you take on a role — parent, doctor, teacher, employee, friend — that role comes with built-in obligations. A parent has an obligation to care for their child. A doctor has an obligation to try to help their patient. These arise not because of a single agreement but because of what that role means in society.

5. Receiving a Benefit
Sometimes, being given something creates an obligation to give something back. If someone does you a great favour, many people feel a social obligation to return the kindness. This is the basis of reciprocity in human relationships.
The Key Characteristics of an Obligation

Understanding these features helps you recognise an obligation precisely:

  • It is binding. An obligation is not a suggestion. It is something you are supposed to do, and there is some kind of pull or pressure behind it.
  • It implies a corresponding right in someone else. When you have an obligation, there is usually someone else (a person, a group, society, or an institution) who has the right to expect that action from you. Your obligation is their entitlement.
  • Failing to fulfil it has consequences. These consequences may be legal (fines, punishment), social (loss of trust, damage to reputation), emotional (guilt, shame), or relational (a damaged friendship or relationship).
  • It exists independently of your feelings. You might not feel like doing it. But an obligation is still an obligation. Your feelings do not dissolve it. This is what distinguishes it from a mere preference or desire.

These words are close in meaning but carry subtle differences:

Obligation vs. Duty
A duty is very similar, but it tends to carry a more formal, official, or role-based flavour. A soldier has a duty to protect their country. A judge has a duty to be impartial. Obligation is broader and more everyday — it covers duties, but also personal promises, social expectations, and moral pressures. You can say someone has an obligation to call their mother, but saying they have a duty to call their mother sounds stiffer and more formal.

Obligation vs. Responsibility
A responsibility is something you are accountable for — it often implies ownership and care. You are responsible for the outcome. An obligation is about what you are required to do. The two often overlap — a parent is both responsible for their child and obligated to care for them — but responsibility is a broader sense of ownership, while obligation is a more specific requirement to act.

Obligation vs. Commitment
A commitment is something you have chosen and pledged yourself to — it is more about personal dedication and follow-through. An obligation can arise without your choice (a legal duty, for instance). A commitment is always voluntarily entered into. When you commit to something, it often creates an obligation.

Legal obligation — Required by law. Paying taxes, appearing in court when summoned, following a signed contract.

Moral obligation — Required by your conscience and ethics, even when no law enforces it. Telling the truth to someone who trusts you. Helping a person in distress when you can easily do so.

Social obligation — Required by the unwritten norms of society and social relationships. Thanking someone for a gift. Attending a close friend's wedding. Responding when someone greets you. These are not laws, but violating them is seen as rude or disrespectful.

Contractual obligation — Specifically required by a formal written or verbal agreement. An employer has a contractual obligation to pay their employees. A tenant has a contractual obligation to pay rent.

Filial obligation — The obligation children have toward their parents, particularly as they grow older — a concept deeply felt in many cultures.
When Is Something NOT an Obligation?

This matters just as much as knowing what an obligation is.

  • If you do something purely out of generosity or kindness, with no expectation or agreement behind it, it is not an obligation — it is a favour or a gift.
  • If you have the option to do something but face no consequence for not doing it, and no one has a right to expect it from you, it is not an obligation — it is a choice.
  • If someone is asking you to do something but has no basis for requiring it from you — no promise, no rule, no relationship that demands it — they may want you to do it, but it is not your obligation.

People sometimes use the phrase "I feel obligated" to describe social pressure that makes them feel like they should do something, even when no true obligation exists. This is an important nuance — feeling obligated and being obligated are not always the same thing.

Obligations carry psychological weight. When you fulfil an obligation, especially a difficult one, it brings a sense of integrity and trustworthiness. When you fail to fulfil one, it typically produces guilt or shame — internal signals that your actions did not match what was expected of you.

Some obligations feel light and easy. Others feel heavy and burdensome — especially when they conflict with your own desires or when they pile up. A person can be overwhelmed by obligations, meaning they have more demands on them than they can comfortably handle.

There is also the concept of obligation without gratitude — sometimes people fulfil obligations that the other person barely notices or never thanks them for. The obligation still existed and still had to be met.

• "Under an obligation" — You are in a position where you owe someone something or must do something for them. "I am under no obligation to explain myself."
  • "A sense of obligation" — A feeling that you should do something, often because of a relationship or past favour.
  • "Meet / fulfil an obligation" — To successfully do what was required of you.
  • "Discharge an obligation" — A more formal phrase meaning to fully complete and therefore eliminate the obligation.
  • "No obligation" — Often used in commercial contexts to mean you can take or try something without being bound to buy or commit. "Try it free, with no obligation."
  • "Mutual obligation" — Both parties owe something to each other.

At the heart of the word obligation is the idea that we are not isolated individuals — we exist in relationships, in societies, under rules, and within roles. Obligations are the ties that hold all of this together. They make trust possible: because I know you are obligated to keep your promise, I can rely on you. Because a contract creates obligations, business can function. Because moral obligations exist, we care for each other beyond mere self-interest.

Without obligations, every action would be entirely optional, and social life as we know it would fall apart.

In short: an obligation is a binding requirement to act, arising from a promise, law, relationship, role, or moral principle — one that exists regardless of your immediate feelings, and whose neglect carries real consequences.
11231:
If something is obligatory, it means you must do it. You have no real choice in the matter. It is required of you — either by a rule, a law, a duty, or a strong social expectation.

Think of it this way: the opposite of obligatory is optional. Optional means you can choose. Obligatory means the choice has already been made for you.

Imagine your school says every student must attend the morning assembly. It is not something you can skip. It is not a suggestion. It is a rule. In that case, attending the assembly is obligatory.

Now imagine the school also has an art club you can join if you want, but nobody is forcing you. That is optional — the total opposite of obligatory.

Obligatory always carries that sense of: you don't get to decide whether to do this or not. It is expected, required, or demanded of you.
The Three Situations Where "Obligatory" Is Used

1. Legal or Official Rules

When a law, regulation, or official authority demands something, that thing is obligatory.

  • Wearing a seatbelt is obligatory in most countries.
  • Military service is obligatory for all citizens above 18 in some nations.
  • Disclosing your income to the tax department is obligatory.

Here, if you fail to do the obligatory thing, there are consequences — a fine, punishment, or legal trouble.

2. Moral or Social Duty

Sometimes, an unwritten social rule or a moral expectation makes something feel obligatory, even if no law forces you. Society, culture, or basic decency demands it.

  • When someone holds the door open for you, a thank-you feels obligatory — not saying it would seem rude.
  • At a funeral, wearing sombre, dark clothing is considered obligatory in many cultures.
  • When you make a mistake at work, an apology to your colleague feels obligatory.

Nobody will arrest you for skipping these, but people will judge you, and your own conscience may trouble you. The "force" here comes from social norms and moral expectation, not a written law.

3. The Informal, Slightly Ironic Use

This is a very interesting and common use of the word. When something has become so predictable, so routine, so expected in a particular context that it almost feels like a rule — even though it technically isn't one — people call it obligatory. This is often said with a light, dry, or even humorous tone.

  • "The action movie had the obligatory car chase scene." (Every action movie seems to have one — it's almost a rule of the genre.)
  • "He gave the obligatory birthday speech." (Everyone at the party expected it; it would have been strange if he hadn't.)
  • "She posted the obligatory holiday selfie." (Everyone does it; it's become almost a cultural routine.)

In this use, you're not saying there is a real rule. You're saying something has become so standard and expected that it feels like one. There's often a hint of "of course, what else would you expect?" in this usage.

Not all obligations are equal, and "obligatory" can reflect different strengths of "must":

  • A legal obligatory duty (e.g., paying taxes) is the strongest — break it and face punishment.
  • A social or moral obligatory expectation (e.g., thanking someone for a gift) is strong but unenforceable — break it and face social disapproval or guilt.
  • The informal/ironic use (e.g., the obligatory chase scene) is the lightest — it just means something is so expected it feels like a rule, even though it isn't.

These words are close cousins, but they are not identical:

Obligatory vs. Mandatory: These are very close in meaning and often interchangeable. However, mandatory tends to appear more in formal, legal, or official settings ("mandatory sentencing," "mandatory training"). Obligatory is slightly wider and works naturally in social and informal contexts too — especially in the ironic third sense described above.

Obligatory vs. Compulsory: Again, very close. Compulsory is especially common in educational contexts ("compulsory subjects," "compulsory education"). Obligatory is more versatile.

Obligatory vs. Necessary: This is an important distinction. Necessary means something is needed for a reason — it might be a practical need, a logical requirement, or a natural dependency. "Water is necessary for survival." But obligatory means something is required by a rule, duty, or expectation. You would not say "water is obligatory for survival" — that would sound odd, because no one has passed a rule demanding you drink water. You would say it is necessary.
One Key Idea to Remember Always

The heart of the word is an outside force demanding something of you — whether that force is a law, a social norm, a cultural tradition, or the predictable pattern of a genre or situation. Whenever something is obligatory, the demand is coming from outside yourself, not from your own personal wish or preference.

If you want to do something, that's desire. If you need to do something practically, that's necessity. But if a rule, a duty, or a strong expectation is making you do it — that is when you reach for obligatory.
Obligatory = You must. No real choice. Something outside you is demanding it.
11232:
Oblige is about being bound — either because something forces you, or because you choose to bind yourself to someone by helping them. These two ideas sound different, but they share the same soul: a sense of duty or commitment pulling you toward an action.

The verb has two main meanings, and both are widely used in everyday English.
Meaning 1: To Require or Compel Someone to Do Something

When a law, rule, circumstance, or moral duty forces you to do something, it obliges you to do it. You have no real choice — something external is pushing you.

Examples:

  • The law obliges all drivers to carry a valid license.
  • The sudden rain obliged us to cancel the picnic.
  • Her position as a doctor obliges her to keep patient information confidential.

In each case, something outside the person — a law, the weather, a professional duty — is doing the "obliging." The person must act because of it.

This meaning is closely related to words like compel, require, force, and bind. The difference is that "oblige" carries a slightly more formal, dignified tone. It doesn't always mean physical force — it often means a moral or legal pressure that a reasonable person is expected to follow.

The Very Common Passive Form: "be obliged to"

You will almost always see this meaning in the passive voice — "be obliged to do something."

  • I am obliged to inform you that your application was rejected.
  • They were obliged to pay a fine.
  • She felt obliged to apologize.

Notice that last one — "felt obliged." This is important. You can feel obliged not just because a law says so, but because your own conscience or social pressure says so. Nobody is holding a gun to your head, but the situation makes you feel you must act. This is one of the subtler, very human uses of the word.
Meaning 2: To Do Someone a Favor or Help Them

This meaning is almost the opposite in feel. Here, you are the one doing the "obliging" — you are doing something kind, helpful, or accommodating for someone else, usually because they asked.

Examples:

  • Could you oblige me by turning down the music?
  • He asked for a glass of water, and she was happy to oblige.
  • The chef obliged the guests with a special dish not on the menu.

When you oblige someone, you are essentially saying: "You needed something, and I came through for you." It has a warm, gracious quality to it. It suggests willingness, helpfulness, and a certain elegance.

The phrase "happy to oblige" is extremely common and worth memorizing — it's a polite, slightly formal way of saying "of course, no problem, I'll do it gladly."

When someone does you a favor, you are left feeling obliged — meaning indebted or grateful to them. This is where the famous phrase "much obliged" comes from. It simply means "thank you very much."

  • "Here's your coat." — "Much obliged."

This usage is somewhat old-fashioned and formal today, but you will still encounter it in literature, period dramas, and among older speakers. Understanding it helps you feel the word's deeper logic: if someone obliges you by helping you, you naturally feel obliged (grateful) to them in return.
How the Two Main Meanings Connect

It might seem strange that one word means both "to force" and "to help," but think of it this way:

Both meanings involve a kind of binding commitment. In Meaning 1, a rule or circumstance binds you to act. In Meaning 2, you bind yourself to another person by choosing to help them. The thread running through both is: something is owed, and it gets fulfilled.

"Oblige" is a moderately formal word. It's not overly stiff or academic, but it sits a notch above casual. You'd use it in professional writing, polite conversation, formal emails, or literature. In everyday casual talk, people might instead say "forced to," "had to," "help out," or "do a favor" — but "oblige" is never out of place in normal conversation either.

SituationWhat "oblige" means
  • A rule or circumstance forces you → it obliges you to do it.
  • You feel internally pressured by conscience or social expectation → you feel obliged to act.
  • You do something helpful or kind for someone who asked → you oblige them.
  • Someone helped you and you feel grateful → you feel obliged (thankful), or you say "much obliged."
Putting It All Together — A Mini Story

Maria was a nurse, and the hospital rules obliged her to report any unusual medication activity. One evening, a nervous new doctor asked her to walk him through the procedure. Though it was the end of her long shift, she obliged willingly — she liked helping newcomers. The doctor looked at her with relief. "Much obliged," he said quietly. Walking home, Maria felt that warm sense of having done what she was both obliged to do by her values, and glad to do by her heart.

In that short story, you can see all three shades of the word working together naturally.
11233:
When "obliged" is used as an adjective, it describes a state of feeling compelled to do something — not by physical force, but by an inner sense of duty, conscience, gratitude, or moral/social pressure. You feel that you must act, even if no one is literally making you.

Think of it as an invisible weight on your conscience saying: "It would be wrong not to do this."

1. Feeling duty-bound or compelled

This is the most common use. You feel obliged when your conscience, sense of responsibility, social expectation, or gratitude makes you feel you have no real moral choice but to act — even if you'd prefer not to.

  • "She felt obliged to attend the funeral, even though she barely knew the family." (social/moral duty)
  • "He was obliged to report the accident to his manager." (professional responsibility)
  • "After everything they had done for her, she felt obliged to help them in return." (gratitude-driven duty)

Notice: nobody is physically forcing these people. But something — conscience, duty, social expectation, or gratitude — makes them feel they have to act. That inner pull is the heart of the word.

2. Feeling grateful (the "much obliged" sense)

In this second meaning, "obliged" means grateful or indebted. This usage is older and more formal. You'll mostly see it in formal writing or older texts, rarely in everyday casual talk.

  • "I am most obliged to you for your assistance." (= I am very grateful to you)
  • "Much obliged!" (= Thank you very much!)
  • "I am obliged to you for pointing that out." (= I am grateful to you for...)

Why are duty and gratitude connected in one word? Because when someone does something kind for you, it creates a moral debt — you now feel you owe them something. This feeling of moral indebtedness links both meanings: in the first meaning, the debt pushes you toward action; in the second meaning, you acknowledge the debt by expressing thanks.
The Most Important Nuance: Internal, Not External

This is the single most important thing to understand about "obliged." The compulsion it describes comes from within — from your own conscience, values, sense of fairness, or feelings of gratitude. It is not the same as being physically forced or ordered by an authority.

Compare:

  • "He was forced to sign the papers at gunpoint." — Physical, external compulsion.
  • "He felt obliged to sign the papers because it was the right thing to do." — Moral, internal compulsion.

This inner quality gives "obliged" a slightly softer, more dignified feel than words like "forced" or "compelled."

"Obliged" sits on a spectrum between "I'd like to" and "I absolutely must."

  • It is stronger than "I should" — you feel a real, pressing pull, not just a vague suggestion.
  • It is softer than "I was forced to" — you technically had a choice, but walking away would have felt morally wrong.

The best way to capture it: "I feel I have no real moral choice but to do this."
A Polite Formula: "I Would Be Obliged If..."

There is a very formal, polite construction using "obliged": "I would be obliged if you could/would..."

This means: "I would be grateful if you could do this for me." It is a courteous way to make a request, mostly found in formal letters or professional correspondence.

  • "I would be obliged if you could send the documents by Thursday."
  • "I would be obliged if you would kindly keep this matter confidential."

Note the difference:

  • "I am obliged" → you already feel the duty or gratitude (present fact).
  • "I would be obliged" → you will feel grateful if the other person does what you're asking (a conditional, forward-looking request).
How It Differs from Similar Words

Obliged vs. Obligated
These are nearly identical and often used interchangeably. However, there is a subtle difference in feel:

  • "Obligated" tends to sound more formal and is better suited to legal, contractual, or official duties.
  • "Obliged" feels more personal, emotional, and social.
    • "He was obligated to repay the loan by law." → "obligated" sounds natural (legal/official)
    • "She felt obliged to comfort her grieving friend." → "obliged" sounds natural (personal/emotional)

In practice, many people use them without distinction, and this is generally accepted.

Obliged vs. Compelled
"Compelled" is stronger. When you are compelled, the urge is almost irresistible. "Obliged" leaves a little more room — you could technically walk away, but your conscience won't let you. "Compelled" suggests the pull was overwhelming.

Obliged vs. Required
"Required" is more external — someone else is demanding something of you (a rule, a person, a system). "Obliged" is more internal — you feel the pull from within yourself, not because someone issued a demand.

Obliged vs. Duty-bound
Very similar in the sense of duty, but "duty-bound" is more formal and old-fashioned. "Obliged" is more versatile and commonly used today.
Register: When and Where Is This Word Used?

"Obliged" is a moderately formal word. You will find it most naturally in:

  • Formal writing and professional correspondence
  • Literature, especially older texts
  • Polite, educated speech

In casual conversation, people tend to say "I felt I had to" or "I had no choice" rather than "I felt obliged." That said, "obliged" is not so stiff that it sounds strange in normal conversation — it fits comfortably in any context without sounding pretentious.

"Obliged" as an adjective describes two related states:

  1. Feeling duty-bound or compelled — by conscience, responsibility, social expectation, or gratitude — where walking away would feel morally wrong. (The most common use.)
  2. Feeling grateful — acknowledging a moral debt to someone who has helped you. (More formal/old-fashioned; "much obliged," "I am obliged to you.")

The word captures an invisible moral weight — not physical force, not an external order — but the kind of inner pressure that your own values and sense of right and wrong place on you. When you are obliged, you feel you simply must act, because not doing so would sit badly with your conscience.
11234:
When you describe someone as obliging, you mean they are willing and eager to help — they do what others need or ask without making a fuss, and they do it with a pleasant, cooperative attitude.

An obliging person doesn't wait to be convinced. They don't help reluctantly or with a sigh. They step forward readily, adjust to what you need, and make things easier for you.

Think of it this way: some people, when asked for help, drag their feet, say "I'm busy," or help but make you feel like a burden. An obliging person is the opposite of that. They are:

  • Willing — they have no problem saying yes
  • Helpful — they actually do something useful for you
  • Cheerful about it — there's no resentment or reluctance in the way they help

So the word captures not just what someone does (helping), but how they do it (willingly, pleasantly, without making it difficult).

• "The hotel receptionist was very obliging — she arranged a late checkout without any hesitation."
    → She didn't argue or push back. She simply made it happen.
  • "He was an obliging neighbour who would fix things around the house whenever anyone needed it."
    → He was the kind of person who made himself useful and available.
  • "The shop assistant was so obliging that she went to the stockroom three times to find the right size."
    → She went above and beyond without being asked or forced to.
  • "I found the staff at the library obliging and patient with all my questions."
    → They were cooperative, easy to deal with, and accommodating.
The tone and feel of the word

"Obliging" is a warm, positive word. When you call someone obliging, you are giving them a compliment. You're saying they make life easier for others.

It also carries a slight sense of good nature — it's not just about doing a task, it's about the person's character. An obliging person is, in some sense, wired to accommodate others. It feels natural for them to help.
A subtle shade of meaning to know

Sometimes, "obliging" can hint that someone is perhaps too eager to please — that they almost never say no, even when they probably should. Used this way, it's not quite a criticism, but a gentle observation.

For example: "He was so obliging that he agreed to take on extra work even when he was already exhausted."

Here, you admire the willingness but also feel a little sorry for the person. This shade of meaning is less common, but worth knowing. In most everyday uses, the word is simply a compliment.
How it differs from similar words

Several words are close to "obliging," but each has a slightly different focus:

  • Helpful — the most general term. Just means someone assists you. It says nothing about their attitude.
  • Accommodating — focuses on flexibility: they adjust to your needs, change their plans, bend the rules a little if needed. Similar to obliging, but leans more toward adapting rather than actively helping.
  • Cooperative — focuses on working with you rather than against you. More neutral in tone; used in teamwork or formal settings.
  • Amenable — means open and agreeable to what's being suggested. More passive; it means they won't resist, but doesn't quite suggest they'll actively go out of their way.
  • Gracious — focuses on being warm and polite in manner, but doesn't necessarily mean they help or accommodate you.
  • Obliging — combines willingness, helpfulness, and a positive attitude all at once. It's the richest of these words when it comes to describing someone who genuinely makes themselves useful to others without any fuss.

The clearest antonyms are:

  • Unaccommodating — unwilling to adjust or help
  • Unhelpful — simply not useful when you need them
  • Obstructive — actively getting in the way
  • Difficult or uncooperative — making things harder rather than easier

"Obliging" has a slightly formal or literary flavour. You're more likely to encounter it in writing — novels, formal reviews, travel writing, or polite descriptions — than in casual speech. A friend might say someone is "really helpful" in conversation, but in writing you might say they were "most obliging."

It is also somewhat more common in British English than in American English, though speakers of both varieties understand it well.

You'll often see it used when describing:

  • People in service roles (staff, assistants, shopkeepers, clerks)
  • Characters in fiction who are agreeable and helpful
  • Someone's general personality or disposition
Obliging describes a person who is readily and cheerfully willing to help, accommodate others' needs, and do what is asked of them — without reluctance, complaint, or difficulty.
11235:
The single idea at the heart of "oblique" is: not straight or direct — going at an angle, or hinting at something instead of saying it plainly.

Everything this word means flows from that one core idea. It has two main areas of meaning: one physical (about direction and shape), and one communicative (about how people express things).
Meaning 1: Physical — Slanting, at an Angle

When something is oblique in a physical sense, it is tilted or slanted rather than straight up-and-down (vertical) or straight across (horizontal). It goes in a diagonal or angled direction.

Think of a "/" or "\" symbol. That line is oblique — it leans at an angle. It is not standing straight up, and it is not lying flat. It cuts across at a slant.

Examples:

  • Rain falling straight down is vertical. Rain blown sideways by wind falls in an oblique direction — at a slant.
  • A "/" mark on a road sign is an oblique line.
  • A knife making a straight-across cut is perpendicular. A knife making a diagonal cut across a vegetable is making an oblique cut.

In geometry, an oblique angle is simply any angle that is not a right angle (not exactly 90°). 45°, 30°, 120° — these are all oblique angles. Two lines are oblique to each other if they are neither parallel (running side by side, never meeting) nor perpendicular (meeting at a perfect 90°).

In your body, you actually have muscles called obliques — the muscles on the sides of your abdomen that run diagonally across your torso. They're named obliques precisely because of the angled direction of their fibers.

This is where the word gets especially rich and interesting.

When a person's words, remarks, or approach are oblique, they are not direct. Instead of saying something plainly and openly, they circle around it, hint at it, or approach it from the side — like taking a slanted path to reach a destination instead of a straight road.

Think of it this way: imagine you want to tell your friend you are unhappy with their behavior, but instead of saying "I'm upset with you," you say, "I just think it's strange how some people forget about their friends when they get busy." You haven't said what you mean directly. You've approached it at an angle. That is an oblique remark.

More examples:

  • A journalist who doesn't openly accuse a politician of lying, but instead writes, "the minister's account raises some curious questions" — that is an oblique criticism.
  • A boss who, instead of saying "your work quality is poor," says "I wonder if some team members might benefit from revisiting their standards" — that's oblique feedback.
  • A character in a novel who never directly says they are in love, but makes oblique references to the person they adore — hinting without confessing.
The Important Nuance: Why Would Someone Be Oblique?

Being oblique in speech is rarely random. People are oblique for specific reasons:

To be polite or gentle. Saying something directly can feel harsh or blunt. An oblique approach softens a difficult message.

To avoid conflict or risk. If you're afraid to say something directly — because it might cause anger, embarrassment, or trouble — you say it obliquely instead. You get your meaning across but give yourself cover if challenged.

To be subtle or sophisticated. In literature, art, and intellectual conversation, being too direct can feel clumsy. A skilled writer might make an oblique reference to an idea, trusting the reader to pick it up without spelling it out.

To be evasive or deceptive. Sometimes people are oblique because they don't want to be pinned down or held accountable. A politician might answer a tough question obliquely — addressing the theme but never truly answering it.

So "oblique" in communication carries a subtle negative undertone in many contexts — it can suggest someone is being slippery, evasive, or unwilling to be fully honest. But not always — sometimes it's simply tact, restraint, or artfulness.
The Thread That Ties It All Together

Whether physical or communicative, "oblique" always means the same fundamental thing: something that does not go straight to its point or destination. A line that slants. A comment that hints. A path that angles. The word describes anything that deviates from the direct, the perpendicular, the straight-on.

DirectOblique
A lineVertical or horizontalSlanted, diagonal
An angleExactly 90°Anything other than 90°
A remark"I disagree with you.""Well, some might see it differently..."
A criticism"That was wrong.""One wonders about the wisdom of that choice."

Once you absorb the core idea — not straight, not direct, going at an angle — you will recognize "oblique" instantly in every context you encounter it, whether in a geometry textbook, a newspaper column, a novel, or a conversation about someone who just couldn't bring themselves to say what they really meant.
11236:
"Obliquely" means not directly — either in a physical direction (not in a straight line, but at an angle) or in the way something is said or done (not plainly, but through hints, suggestions, or a roundabout approach).

Think of it as the opposite of going straight at something — whether that "something" is a physical direction or a point you're trying to make.

1. Physical / Literal Sense — At a slant or angle

When something moves, falls, is positioned, or happens at an angle rather than straight on, it happens obliquely.

"The afternoon sun shone obliquely through the blinds, casting long diagonal shadows across the floor."

Here, the sunlight isn't falling straight down or hitting the floor head-on — it's coming in at a slant.

"She was standing obliquely to the door, half-turned away."

She isn't facing the door directly — her body is angled.

This sense is common in technical fields — optics (light hitting a surface obliquely), anatomy (muscles running obliquely across the body), and geometry (a line cutting obliquely through another line at a non-right angle).

2. Figurative / Communicative Sense — Indirectly, without saying it plainly

This is the far more common use in everyday English. When someone says or does something obliquely, they are deliberately avoiding directness — hinting, suggesting, or implying something rather than stating it outright.

"She obliquely suggested that he wasn't qualified for the job."

She didn't say "You're not qualified." She hinted at it — maybe by emphasizing the experience the role requires, or by mentioning someone else's strong credentials. The message got through, but it wasn't stated openly.

"He obliquely criticized the government's policy in his speech."

He didn't attack it head-on. He spoke around it — through analogies, comparisons, or carefully chosen words that make his disapproval clear to a listening ear without him ever saying "this policy is wrong."
Why Do People Speak or Act Obliquely?

This is where it gets interesting. Someone acts obliquely for one of a few reasons:

1. To be polite or tactful. Directly saying "Your work is poor" feels harsh. Saying obliquely, "I wonder if the approach could be refined a little," softens the message while still communicating it.

2. To protect themselves. If you criticize something directly, you own that criticism fully. Speaking obliquely gives you plausible deniability — "I didn't say that, I only implied..."

3. To test the waters. Before committing to a position, people sometimes raise an idea obliquely to see how others react — without putting themselves fully on the line.

4. To be subtle or sophisticated. In literature, politics, or intellectual discourse, oblique references can be a sign of nuance — a preference for suggestion over bluntness.
The Key Feeling of the Word

When you encounter obliquely, ask yourself: "Is something going at an angle — physically or communicatively?"

  • A slanted beam of light → oblique direction
  • A veiled criticism that never names its target → oblique communication

The underlying flavour is always the same: something is coming at you sideways, not straight on.

• Oblique ≠ vague. Something vague is unclear or fuzzy. Something oblique can be very pointed and clear in its meaning — it just reaches you through an indirect route. A well-placed oblique remark can sting just as much as a direct one; you just can't quote it back as easily.
  • Oblique ≠ dishonest. Speaking obliquely isn't the same as lying. The information is present — it just isn't handed to you on a plate. You have to read between the lines.
  • It often implies intent. When someone does something obliquely, there's usually a reason they chose not to be direct. The word quietly implies awareness and choice, not accident.

Words that mean something similar:

  • Indirectly
  • In a roundabout way
  • Allusively (by allusion)
  • Sideways (in physical contexts)
  • Diagonally (in physical/spatial contexts)

Words that are the opposite:

  • Directly
  • Straightforwardly
  • Bluntly
  • Head-on
  • Squarely
A Few More Examples to Cement It

"The journalist obliquely accused the minister of corruption without ever using that word."

"Light entering a pool of water obliquely bends as it crosses into the denser medium."

"Rather than asking outright, she obliquely brought up how expensive city apartments had become — her real question being whether he could afford the rent."

"He glanced at her obliquely, not wanting her to catch him looking."
"Obliquely" means at an angle — whether that angle is physical (a slanting direction) or figurative (an indirect, roundabout way of saying or doing something).
11237: Obliquity means the quality or state of not being straight. Think of a straight line going perfectly horizontal or vertical. Anything that tilts, slants, or deviates from that straight path has obliquity. That's the seed of the word — and from that one physical idea, the meaning branches out in several important directions.
1. The Physical Meaning — Literal Slant or Tilt

In its most literal sense, obliquity describes the degree to which something is angled or tilted away from a straight, upright, or expected position.

If you place a book perfectly upright, it has no obliquity. If you tilt it, the tilt itself — that deviation from straight — is its obliquity.

"The obliquity of the leaning tower was visible from miles away."

In geometry, if two lines are not parallel and not perpendicular (i.e., they meet at some unusual angle), the angle between them can be described as their obliquity.

This is one of the most famous and specific uses of the word. Scientists talk about the obliquity of the ecliptic, which refers to the tilt of Earth's axis relative to the flat plane of Earth's orbit around the Sun.

Earth doesn't spin perfectly upright. It leans at about 23.5 degrees. That lean is its obliquity. And it matters enormously — this tilt is the reason we have seasons. When the Northern Hemisphere tilts toward the Sun, it gets summer. When it tilts away, it gets winter.

Without obliquity, there would be no seasons. Every day of the year would feel the same at each location on Earth.

Other planets have their own obliquity too:

  • Uranus has an obliquity of about 98 degrees — it essentially rolls around the Sun on its side.
  • Mars has an obliquity close to Earth's, which is why it also experiences seasons.
3. The Communicative Meaning — Indirectness in Speech or Writing

Here the word moves into human behavior. When a person does not say something directly — when they hint, suggest, talk around a subject, or approach a point from an angle instead of head-on — that indirectness is called obliquity.

Imagine you ask someone: "Did you take my money?"

A direct answer: "No, I didn't."

An oblique answer: "I've always respected other people's belongings. You know, my mother raised me to be honest."

That second answer never actually answers the question. It circles around it. That sly, slanting quality — avoiding the straight path of direct speech — is obliquity.

"The politician's obliquity frustrated journalists who wanted simple answers."

Sometimes obliquity in communication is deliberately deceptive. Other times, it's used tactfully — to soften difficult truths, to be diplomatic, or to hint at something that feels too blunt to say outright. Whether it is cunning or polite depends on the context.

In literature, writers sometimes use obliquity on purpose — approaching a painful or complex subject indirectly because a head-on approach would feel too harsh or too simple. A poem about grief might never mention death directly; its obliquity is part of its artistry.
4. The Moral Meaning — Deviation from Virtue or Right Conduct

This is the most serious and weighty use of the word. Morally, obliquity refers to a departure from what is honest, upright, or ethical. Just as a tilted line deviates from straight, a morally oblique person deviates from virtue.

Think of moral obliquity as ethical crookedness — not necessarily outright villainy, but a quiet turning away from what is right. Dishonesty, evasion of responsibility, self-serving twisting of the truth — these are all forms of moral obliquity.

"The scandal revealed years of obliquity in the company's financial reporting."

"He was a man of such moral obliquity that he could lie without the slightest discomfort."

The word carries a slightly formal, serious tone here. It suggests not just a single bad act, but a tendency or character trait of being morally crooked.
5. The Mental Meaning — Distorted or Confused Thinking

Less commonly, obliquity can describe a deviation from clear, sound, or logical reasoning. When someone's thinking is twisted, confused, or biased in a way that prevents them from seeing things clearly, that distortion of mind can be called obliquity.

"The obliquity of his reasoning made it impossible to follow his argument."

This usage treats the mind like a lens — a straight, uncorrupted mind sees clearly, but obliquity in thinking introduces a slant that bends one's perception of reality.

All the meanings of obliquity share one unifying idea: a deviation from the straight, the direct, or the upright — whether that deviation is:

  • Physical (a tilt or slant in an object or angle),
  • Astronomical (the tilt of a planet's axis),
  • Communicative (indirectness or evasiveness in speech),
  • Moral (a departure from honesty and virtue), or
  • Mental (a distortion in reasoning or perception).

The word always carries the image of something that should be straight but isn't. That core image — the angled, the tilted, the not-quite-direct — is what gives obliquity its meaning across all contexts.

Obliquity is a formal, somewhat literary word. When you use it, you signal careful and precise thinking. In moral and communicative contexts, it usually carries a slightly negative connotation — suggesting something evasive, questionable, or untrustworthy. In scientific contexts (especially astronomy), it is entirely neutral and technical.

The opposite of obliquity, in almost every sense, is directness — of angle, of speech, of character, of thought.
11238:
To obliterate something means to destroy it so completely that nothing — or almost nothing — is left behind. Not just damaged. Not just broken. Gone. Wiped out entirely.

This is the heart of the word, and the detail that separates it from simpler words like "destroy" or "damage." When something is obliterated, the result is near-total absence. Think of it as destruction taken all the way to the finish line.

If you destroy a sandcastle, it's knocked down — it's ruined. But if you obliterate a sandcastle, you stomp it flat, scatter the sand, and smooth the beach over so that no one walking by would ever know a sandcastle had existed there. The difference is that obliterate carries the sense of erasing all evidence, not just causing damage or ruin.

This is why obliterate is one of the strongest words in English for expressing total annihilation. Writers and speakers choose it deliberately when they want to emphasize that something is not just gone — it is as if it never was.
The Three Main Ways It Is Used

1. Physical destruction

This is the most straightforward use. A powerful force wipes out something in the real, physical world.

  • The volcanic eruption obliterated the entire village.
  • The explosion obliterated the building, leaving nothing but a crater.
  • Decades of wind and rain had nearly obliterated the ancient carvings on the stone.

Notice that the cause can be a weapon, a natural disaster, time, or any force powerful enough to leave little or nothing behind.

2. Erasing something abstract

Obliterate is used very naturally when talking about things that aren't physical — like memories, feelings, records, or differences between things.

  • Years of therapy helped her obliterate the painful memories.
  • The new discovery obliterated every scientific theory that came before it.
  • Grief had obliterated his ability to think clearly.

Here, the word still carries the same core idea — something has been so thoroughly erased or overridden that it might as well no longer exist.

3. Defeating someone overwhelmingly (informal)

In casual speech, sports commentary, and gaming, obliterate is often used hyperbolically to mean a defeat so decisive it felt like total destruction.

  • We obliterated the other team — it was 9 to 0.
  • She obliterated her competition and took first place by a huge margin.

This use is informal and slightly exaggerated, but it is widely understood and commonly used. It is not wrong — it simply lives in a less formal register.

Obliterate is a transitive verb, which means it always needs an object — something being obliterated. You would never say "the bomb obliterated" and stop there. You would say "the bomb obliterated the bridge." There must always be a target.

It works naturally in the passive voice too:

  • The records were obliterated in the fire.
  • All traces of the city had been obliterated by the time archaeologists arrived.
The Feeling and Tone of the Word

Obliterate is not a neutral word. It is intense, dramatic, and final. When you use it, you are signaling that whatever happened was not partial — it was absolute. This makes it a powerful word in writing and speech when you want your reader or listener to feel the full weight of a total loss or total defeat.

Because of this intensity, it is often found in serious contexts — war reporting, history books, dramatic fiction — but also in casual, energetic speech when people want to express that something was done in an overwhelming way.

Obliterate means →to destroy so completely that little or no trace remains
Used for →physical things, abstract things (memories, ideas, records), and informally for overwhelming defeat
Always needs →an object (something being obliterated)
Tone →strong, final, intense — not a word you use lightly
Key distinguishing idea →it's not just destruction; it's destruction that erases evidence of existence

If you take away one thing: obliterate = destroy so thoroughly that nothing is left. Every use of this word, in any context, is a variation of that single powerful idea.
11239:
Obliteration means the act of wiping something out so completely that virtually nothing of it remains — no trace, no sign, no evidence it ever existed. It is total, absolute destruction or erasure.

Think of it this way: if you crumple a piece of paper and throw it in the bin, that is not obliteration — the paper still exists. If you burn it to ash, that is closer. But obliteration goes even further than that — it is the kind of destruction where even the ash is gone.

The single most important thing to understand about this word is the idea of completeness. Obliteration is not partial damage. It is not "mostly gone." It is entirely gone — erased to the point where the thing in question has ceased to exist in any meaningful, recognisable form.
What Makes It Different From Similar Words

Many words describe destruction, so it helps to understand what sets obliteration apart.

  • Destruction means something is broken or ruined, but it can still leave behind ruins, rubble, or remnants. A destroyed building still has its walls.
  • Demolition means tearing something down deliberately, but again, debris remains.
  • Obliteration is a level beyond both. After obliteration, there is essentially nothing left — no ruins, no remnants worth speaking of, no recognisable form.

Think of the difference like this: a wrecking ball causes destruction. A nuclear explosion causes obliteration.
The Many Situations Where This Word Is Used

This word is not limited to physical destruction. It is used across many different areas of life, and understanding each context will help you recognise and use it with confidence.

1. Physical Destruction

This is the most vivid and literal use. When something physical — a building, a city, an object, a landscape — is completely wiped out with nothing left behind, that is obliteration.

"The volcanic eruption caused the obliteration of the entire village. By morning, there was no sign it had ever been there."

"The army's bombing campaign resulted in the obliteration of the bridge."

2. Erasure of Records, Memories, or Evidence

Obliteration also applies to things that are not physical — like information, memories, or history. When records are destroyed so thoroughly that something is completely wiped from history, or when a memory disappears entirely from someone's mind, that too is obliteration.

"The fire at the archive led to the obliteration of centuries of historical records."

"His illness caused the obliteration of his earliest childhood memories."

This is why you will sometimes hear phrases like "the obliteration of a culture" — meaning a culture was erased so completely that almost nothing of it survived.

3. Complete Defeat (in Sports, Competition, or War)

In less literal, more dramatic usage, obliteration is used when someone or something is defeated so overwhelmingly that they were left with nothing — no chance, no dignity in the score, no way to compete.

"The final score of 9–0 was an obliteration of the opposing team."

"The startup faced obliteration when a tech giant entered the same market."

Here, the word is being used as a powerful exaggeration to convey how one-sided and total the defeat was.

4. Medical Usage

In medicine, obliteration has a precise technical meaning: the complete closing off or blocking of a body cavity, passage, or vessel, so that it no longer exists as an open space. For example, a blood vessel can undergo obliteration, meaning it becomes entirely sealed or closed — no longer functional.

"The scan revealed obliteration of the duct, requiring surgical intervention."

You do not need to memorise the medical details, but it is useful to know this usage exists, so you are not confused when you encounter it in a medical text.

Beyond its definition, obliteration carries a strong emotional and dramatic weight. It is not a neutral word. When someone uses it, they are signalling that the destruction or erasure was not accidental, minor, or partial — it was overwhelming and final. It often implies a sense of shock, scale, or gravity.

This is why writers, journalists, and speakers choose it deliberately when they want to emphasise that something is gone beyond recovery. It has a sense of finality that words like "damage" or "destruction" simply do not have.

Since you are a learner, it helps to see how this word connects to its family:

  • Obliterate — the verb. "The storm obliterated the coastline." (meaning: it wiped it out completely)
  • Obliteration — the noun you are learning. "The obliteration of the town was devastating."
  • Obliterating — the present participle / adjective. "An obliterating defeat."
A Simple One-Line Summary to Remember It By

Obliteration is the complete and total wiping out of something — physical or abstract — so that nothing, or next to nothing, remains.

If you can remember that total erasure is the heart of this word, you will never misuse it or misunderstand it.
11240:
Oblivion means a state of being completely and totally gone — either gone from someone's memory, or gone from one's own awareness of the world. Think of it as the ultimate form of "nothing left." Not a little forgotten. Not almost gone. Completely and utterly erased.

The word has two closely related but distinct meanings, and understanding both will give you full command of it.
Meaning 1: The State of Being Forgotten

This is the most common meaning. Oblivion is the condition where something (or someone) has been so thoroughly forgotten that no trace of it exists in anyone's memory anymore. It's not about you forgetting something — it's about something disappearing from the memory of the entire world.

Think of it this way: if a singer was once famous but nobody remembers them today, not a single person on Earth — they have fallen into oblivion. Their name, their songs, their face — all of it is gone from human memory forever.

Examples:

  • "Many great civilizations of the ancient world have faded into oblivion."
  • "Without his journals, his life story would have been lost to oblivion."
  • "She feared that after her death, her work would simply sink into oblivion."

Notice the phrases used with it: fall into, fade into, sink into, lost to, rescued from — all of these suggest oblivion is like a dark pit or a deep ocean that things disappear into, never to return.
Meaning 2: The State of Being Unaware or Unconscious

This meaning is more personal. Here, oblivion refers to a person's mental state — specifically, a state of being completely unaware, unconscious, or cut off from the world around them. When you are in oblivion, you feel nothing, know nothing, and are aware of nothing.

This can happen through:

  • Deep, dreamless sleep
  • The effect of alcohol or drugs
  • A medical state of unconsciousness
  • Extreme emotional exhaustion

Examples:

  • "He drank himself into oblivion." (He drank so much that he lost all awareness of reality.)
  • "The painkillers sent her into merciful oblivion." (The medication made her unconscious, sparing her from pain.)
  • "After the accident, he slipped into oblivion." (He lost consciousness.)

There is a third use, closely connected to the first two, where oblivion means the state of being completely destroyed — wiped out so thoroughly that nothing at all remains. This is often used in dramatic, high-stakes contexts.

Examples:

  • "The entire village was bombed into oblivion."
  • "One wrong decision could send this company into oblivion."
  • "The asteroid threatened to hurl life on Earth into oblivion."

Here, oblivion isn't just about forgetting or sleeping — it's about total annihilation.
The Thread That Connects All Three Meanings

You might notice that all three meanings share the same soul: total absence. Whether it's absence from memory (being forgotten), absence from awareness (being unconscious), or absence from existence (being destroyed) — oblivion always represents a complete, absolute zero. This is what makes the word so powerful and why writers and speakers reach for it when they want to emphasize that something is thoroughly and irreversibly gone.
The Feeling and Tone of the Word

Oblivion is a formal, literary, and somewhat dramatic word. You won't typically hear it in casual small talk. It carries weight. It sounds serious, even a little dark. When someone uses it, they are signaling that what's being described is not small or trivial — it is total, final, and profound.

It can occasionally be used in a positive or neutral sense (for example, craving oblivion as relief from pain or stress), but more often it carries a somber, melancholic, or even ominous tone.

A few important things to keep in mind:

You don't just "be in oblivion" randomly. Things are usually sent, driven, pushed, fallen, or faded into oblivion. It's a destination — somewhere things go, not something that just casually happens.

It is uncountable. You would never say "an oblivion" or "two oblivions." There is no plural. You simply say oblivion — just as you'd say darkness or silence.

It is typically used without an article. You say "fell into oblivion," not "fell into the oblivion" (though "the oblivion" can appear in poetic or philosophical contexts).

Imagine a vast, silent, empty void — no light, no sound, no memory, no feeling, no existence. That void is oblivion. Anything that enters it is gone completely: forgotten, unconscious, or destroyed. That image will serve you every time you encounter this word.
11241:
Oblivious means being completely unaware of something that is happening around you, or failing to notice something that is fairly obvious or important. When someone is oblivious, their mind is simply not registering a thing — it's as if that thing doesn't exist for them at all, even though it clearly exists for everyone else.

Think of it this way: imagine you are so deeply absorbed in your phone while walking on a busy street that you don't notice a dog barking at you, people rushing past you, or even someone calling your name loudly. In that moment, you are oblivious to all of it. The world around you is fully active, but your mind has tuned it out entirely.
What It Really Means — Going Deeper

The key thing to understand is that oblivious describes a state of the mind, not a choice. A person who is oblivious is not deliberately ignoring something. They genuinely do not notice it or are simply unaware of it. This is an important distinction — "ignoring" something is a conscious decision, but being oblivious to something means it hasn't even registered in your mind in the first place.

For example:

  • She was oblivious to the fact that everyone in the room was staring at her.
  • He kept talking cheerfully, completely oblivious to the tension in the air.

In both cases, the person has no idea something is happening. It's not that they saw it and chose to overlook it — they simply didn't pick up on it at all.

In everyday modern English, oblivious is almost always followed by the word "to":

  • She was oblivious to the noise.
  • He was oblivious to the danger.

You will also sometimes see it followed by "of", which is the older, more formal pattern:

  • She was oblivious of her surroundings.

Both are grammatically correct. However, "oblivious to" is far more common in everyday speech and writing today, so that's the form you'll encounter most and the one you should use.
The Tone and Feel of the Word

Oblivious is a word that carries a slightly negative or critical edge in most situations. When you describe someone as oblivious, you're usually implying that they should have been aware of something but weren't — that their lack of awareness was, in some way, a problem or a shortcoming.

For example:

  • The manager was oblivious to his employees' frustration. — This suggests the manager was not doing his job of paying attention.
  • She walked into the meeting completely oblivious to the conflict that had just erupted. — This implies she was caught off guard due to not being plugged in.

However, oblivious is not always a harsh criticism. Sometimes it's used in a gentler, even affectionate or humorous way:

  • He was happily oblivious to all the party preparations happening behind his back. — Here, his unawareness is sweet and harmless.
  • The baby played on the floor, blissfully oblivious to the chaos around her. — Here, obliviousness is actually described as a kind of peaceful state.

So the tone depends heavily on context. It can range from gently humorous to seriously critical.

Oblivious tends to describe a total or near-total lack of awareness, not a partial one. This is what gives the word its punch. It's a strong word. You wouldn't say someone is "slightly oblivious" the way you might say someone is "slightly distracted." When you call someone oblivious, you're saying they are thoroughly unaware — they missed it completely.

That said, in casual speech, people do use phrases like "a bit oblivious" to soften the word, especially when they don't want to sound too critical. But even then, the core idea of significant unawareness remains.

Understanding how oblivious compares to words with similar meanings will sharpen your understanding of it.

Unaware is the closest synonym and can almost always replace oblivious. It is neutral and factual — it simply states that someone doesn't know something. Oblivious is stronger and often implies that the unawareness is somewhat surprising or notable.

Ignorant means lacking knowledge or information about something. It can be used in a neutral way (ignorant of the new rules) or as an insult. Oblivious is not about lacking knowledge in general — it's specifically about failing to notice or perceive something in a given situation.

Inattentive means not paying attention. It focuses on the act of not paying attention. Oblivious focuses on the result — the complete unawareness that comes from not paying attention.

Absent-minded means forgetting things or being mentally elsewhere due to being deep in thought. An absent-minded person might be oblivious to their surroundings, but absent-mindedness implies a scatter-brained or dreamy quality, whereas obliviousness is broader.

The most natural antonyms of oblivious are aware, conscious, alert, attentive, and mindful. All of these describe a state in which a person is actively tuned in to what is happening around them or to them.
One Sentence to Anchor It All

If you had to lock in the meaning of oblivious in a single sentence, here it is:

Oblivious means being completely unaware of something that is happening, especially when that thing is noticeable or important, and you have no idea it's even there.

Every time you come across the word, ask yourself: Who is unaware of what? The answer will always be right there in the sentence.
11242:
When you call something oblong, you are saying it has an elongated shape — it is noticeably longer in one direction than in the other. It is not a perfect square, and not a perfect circle. One dimension (length, width, or height) clearly dominates the other.

Picture a standard brick. It is much longer than it is tall. That is an oblong shape. Now picture a square tile — equal on all four sides. That is not oblong. The moment one side becomes clearly longer than the other, the shape qualifies as oblong.
Two types of shapes it describes

"Oblong" can describe two broad kinds of shapes:

1. A rectangle that is not a square. A four-sided figure with right angles, but where the length and width are unequal. A sheet of A4 paper, a door, a swimming pool, a standard TV screen — all oblong in this sense.

2. An elongated oval or ellipse. A rounded shape stretched in one direction. An egg is oval, but it is also oblong — clearly longer than it is wide.

So "oblong" is not limited to rectangles. It applies to any shape — straight-edged or curved — as long as it is stretched out along one dimension.

Something can be oblong because it is wide and low (like a long dining table), or because it is tall and narrow (like a tall narrow mirror). Either way, as long as one dimension is clearly longer than the other, the word applies.

• A perfect square → not oblong (all sides equal)
  • A perfect circle → not oblong (equal in every direction)
  • A shape that is roughly as tall as it is wide, with no clearly "longer" direction → not oblong

• "The conference room is oblong — long and narrow, with seats running down both sides."
  • "She had an oblong face, longer than it was wide."
  • "The farmer planted seeds in an oblong patch of soil."
  • "They hung an oblong mirror above the fireplace — it was taller than it was wide."
  • "The pizza came on an oblong tray instead of a round one."

"Oblong" implies a noticeable difference between the two dimensions. If a shape is only very slightly longer than it is wide, people would not typically call it oblong — it would just appear "nearly square" or "nearly circular." The elongation needs to be clearly visible.
How it compares to similar words

• Rectangular is more precise and technical — it means specifically a four-sided shape with four right angles. "Oblong" is more informal and flexible; it covers both rectangular shapes and rounded/oval shapes.
  • Elongated is a close sibling — it means stretched or extended in length. You can often use the two words interchangeably, but "elongated" emphasizes the act of stretching, while "oblong" describes the resulting shape.
  • Oval refers specifically to a smooth, egg-like rounded shape. An oval is oblong (because it is longer than wide), but oblong is not always oval (it can have sharp corners and straight sides).

Oblong = any shape that is clearly longer in one direction than the other. Whether it has sharp corners like a rectangle or smooth curves like an egg does not matter. What makes something oblong is simply that one dimension outweighs the other — the shape is stretched out rather than balanced equally in all directions.
11243:
Obloquy has two closely connected meanings, and the full meaning of the word lives in both of them together.

The first meaning is harsh public verbal condemnation — when someone is spoken about very badly, attacked sharply in words, denounced openly, often by many people at once. Not quiet, private grumbling. Loud, forceful, public disapproval directed at a person.

The second meaning is the state of disgrace and damaged reputation that results from that kind of condemnation — when someone has been so thoroughly denounced that their name is stained, their honor is gone, and society looks down on them as a result.

Think of the two meanings as cause and effect: the fierce public condemnation (the act) and the lasting disgrace that it leaves behind (the result). When you use the word obloquy, you're almost always capturing both at once.

Three qualities define obloquy and make it a very specific kind of thing:

It is public. Obloquy is never a whisper in a corner. It happens out in the open — in newspapers, town squares, public discourse, or among communities. The exposure is part of what makes it so damaging.

It is strong. This is not mild criticism or a polite disagreement. Obloquy is fierce, heavy-handed condemnation — closer to denunciation than to disapproval.

It carries a moral charge. The person subjected to obloquy isn't merely disliked — they are seen as having done something shameful, dishonorable, or wrong. The condemnation isn't just "we don't agree with you." It's "you are a disgrace."

• After the general was exposed for abandoning his troops, he spent the rest of his life under a cloud of obloquy — shunned by former allies and condemned in every account of the war.
  • She had done nothing wrong, yet the obloquy heaped upon her by the press was so severe that she quietly left public life forever.
  • History sometimes redeems those who suffered obloquy in their own time — artists, scientists, and reformers who were mocked and condemned, only to be celebrated by later generations.
  • He accepted the obloquy without complaint, knowing that defending himself publicly would only make things worse.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Since obloquy sits in a neighborhood of words that all deal with condemnation and disgrace, it's worth understanding exactly where it stands.

Criticism is much milder and can be entirely private and constructive. Obloquy is always harsh, always public, and never constructive.

Insult is typically a single, sharp exchange between individuals. Obloquy is sustained, widespread, and social in nature.

Infamy focuses on the state of being widely known for something terrible — the famous-for-bad-reasons quality. Obloquy focuses more on the active process of being condemned in words, as well as the resulting disgrace.

Opprobrium is the word closest to obloquy — they are near-synonyms and often interchangeable. The faint distinction, if any, is that obloquy slightly emphasizes the spoken or written attacks directed at someone, while opprobrium slightly emphasizes the attitude of contempt and scorn that others hold. In practice, most careful writers treat them as equivalent.

Vilification refers specifically to the act of saying terrible things about someone to destroy their reputation. Obloquy covers both that act and the disgrace that results from it, giving it a slightly wider scope.
Register and Tone — When You'll Encounter This Word

Obloquy is a formal, literary word. You will almost never hear it in everyday conversation. You will encounter it in serious, careful writing — historical prose, literary fiction, formal essays, or high-register journalism. It tends to appear when the stakes are significant: political scandal, moral failure, public betrayal, or the ruin of a reputation.

When a writer reaches for obloquy instead of simply writing condemnation or disgrace, they are usually doing so deliberately — to give weight and gravity to what they're describing, and to capture both the verbal attacks and the resulting shame in a single, precise word.
If you had to boil it all down: obloquy is the fierce, public verbal condemnation of a person, and the lasting disgrace that such condemnation brings upon them.
11244:
Obnoxious describes someone or something that is so unpleasant, irritating, or offensive that it actively bothers the people around it. It goes beyond a small irritation — it is the kind of unpleasantness that is hard to ignore, often loud or in-your-face, and makes others feel uncomfortable, annoyed, or disgusted.

Think of it as a stronger, sharper version of "annoying." If something is merely annoying, you notice it and it bothers you a little. If something is obnoxious, it is aggressively, boldly, and persistently unpleasant — it gets in your face and refuses to leave you alone.
The Two Main Ways It Is Used

1. To describe a person's behavior
This is the most common use. When a person is called obnoxious, it means they behave in a way that is socially irritating and offensive to others — often because they are too loud, too rude, too self-centered, too boastful, or too pushy. A key feature here is that the obnoxious person usually doesn't realize how much they are bothering others, or simply doesn't care.

The man at the next table was being obnoxious — he kept interrupting others, talking over everyone, and laughing loudly at his own jokes.

She found her coworker obnoxious because he constantly bragged about himself and never let anyone else speak.

2. To describe a thing (a smell, sound, comment, habit, etc.)
Obnoxious is also used for non-human things — a smell, a noise, a remark, or a behavior — when they are offensively unpleasant and hard to ignore.

The obnoxious smell coming from the garbage truck made everyone on the street turn away.

He made an obnoxious comment at dinner that made the whole table go silent.

The car's obnoxious horn blared through the quiet neighborhood.

It helps to see it on a scale:

Mild → Annoying → Obnoxious → Insufferable / Unbearable

  • Annoying = slightly irritating; you can tolerate it.
  • Obnoxious = strongly, offensively unpleasant; hard to ignore or tolerate; it pushes into your personal space or peace.
  • Insufferable = so unbearable you feel you absolutely cannot stand it.

So "obnoxious" sits in the upper range — it is a serious complaint, not a mild one. When you call someone obnoxious, you are saying more than just "they mildly bother me." You are saying their behavior is genuinely offensive and disruptive.
The Feeling It Creates in Others

The key emotional reaction obnoxious behavior produces in others is a combination of:

  • Irritation (it bothers you)
  • Discomfort (it makes you uneasy or embarrassed)
  • A desire to get away (you don't want to be near it)

This is what separates it from words like "rude" or "mean." Someone rude is disrespectful. Someone mean causes emotional harm. Someone obnoxious is specifically the kind of person who is so aggressively, loudly, or disgustingly unpleasant that you just want to leave the room.

• It does not mean evil or morally wicked. An obnoxious person is irritating and unpleasant — not necessarily a bad or dangerous person at heart.
  • It does not mean quiet, shy, or withdrawn. Obnoxious behavior is almost always noticeable — it draws attention, usually in an unwanted way.
  • It is not as extreme as "horrible" or "terrible" in all cases — those words imply something deeply distressing, whereas obnoxious is more about social irritation and offensiveness.

WordMeaning
  • Annoying is milder than obnoxious. A dripping tap is annoying. A person who won't stop talking about themselves at full volume is obnoxious.
  • Offensive can overlap with obnoxious, but "offensive" often points to something that violates moral or social decency (an offensive joke, for instance). Obnoxious is more about being unpleasantly in-your-face.
  • Insufferable is slightly stronger than obnoxious — it implies you truly cannot bear the person or thing at all.
  • Irritating is milder and more neutral; it lacks the "aggressive unpleasantness" that obnoxious carries.

"Obnoxious" is used in everyday, informal speech as well as in writing. It is a word you might hear in normal conversation, read in a book review, or see in a news article. It is not rude or vulgar to use, but it is a strong word — using it signals real frustration or genuine displeasure, not a light complaint.

Obnoxious means aggressively and offensively unpleasant — the kind of person or thing that boldly, noticeably, and persistently bothers everyone around it, often without any awareness or care that it is doing so.
11245:
When something is obscene, it is so deeply offensive to people's sense of decency and morality that it shocks or disgusts them. It goes beyond just being unpleasant or rude — it violates what most people in a society feel are the basic standards of acceptable human behaviour or expression.

Think of it this way: if something makes you feel not just uncomfortable, but genuinely morally revolted — a feeling of "this should not exist in the world" — that something is likely obscene.

The most common and historically original use of obscene is about sexual content. Something is obscene in this sense when it is graphic, explicit, or lewd in a sexual way that crosses the line most people draw between what is acceptable and what is not.

A pornographic image showing graphic sexual acts is obscene. A scene in a book that describes sex in an extremely explicit and degrading way might be called obscene. Graffiti with graphic sexual drawings on a public school wall is obscene.

What separates obscene from simply "sexual" is the degree of explicitness and the level of moral offence it causes. A romantic kiss in a film is sexual but not obscene. Nudity in fine art is often not considered obscene. Obscene sexual content is the kind that makes most reasonable people feel it has crossed a clear line.

Over time, obscene stretched beyond sexual content. Today, it is very commonly used to describe anything that is so outrageously extreme in amount, scale, or nature that it offends people's sense of fairness, decency, or humanity — even when sex has nothing to do with it.

Some examples of this use:

  • "Obscene wealth" — when a single person owns so much money that it seems morally wrong or deeply unfair to most people.
  • "Obscene profits" — a corporation making enormous profits while people suffer, in a way that feels indecent.
  • "Obscene violence" — violence so brutal and graphic that it shocks beyond what people think is humane or acceptable to witness.
  • "The conditions in that prison were obscene" — meaning the conditions were so inhumane that they offended basic human decency.

The common thread in all these uses: something so excessive, extreme, or wrong that it triggers a moral reaction — a feeling that basic standards of humanity or decency have been violated.
The Key Qualities That Make Something "Obscene"

For something to be called obscene, a few things are usually true:

  1. It crosses a widely accepted moral or social boundary. It is not just unpleasant to one person — it offends what most people in a community or society would consider decent.
  2. It provokes moral disgust, not just discomfort. Being bored by a film is not obscene. Being made to feel morally revolted by graphic content is.
  3. It goes too far. Obscene things are almost always about excess — too explicit, too brutal, too unjust, too degrading.
The Role of Subjectivity and Context

Here is an important and honest fact: what is obscene is not fully fixed. It depends on culture, era, community, and context.

What was considered obscene in one century may be widely accepted in the next. A painting that caused moral outrage in 1880 might hang in a school today. Language that was obscene decades ago appears freely in mainstream entertainment now.

It also varies across societies — what is deeply offensive in one culture may be unremarkable in another.

This does not mean "obscene" is meaningless. It means the word describes a relationship between content and the moral standards of a particular community at a particular time. It is a real judgment, but it is not perfectly objective and universal.

In law, especially in the United States, "obscene" has a precise technical meaning used to determine what kinds of material can be legally banned or regulated. Courts use specific tests — the material must appeal to prurient (sexual) interest, depict sexual conduct in a patently offensive way, and have no serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value. But this legal definition is a specialised use — in everyday language, the word is used more freely and broadly.

It helps to separate obscene from nearby words:

  • Rude or vulgar — these describe crude, ill-mannered, or coarse language/behaviour. Saying a dirty joke at a dinner table is vulgar. It may not be obscene. Obscene implies a stronger moral violation.
  • Offensive — a much broader word. Anything that offends someone can be called offensive. Obscene specifically suggests a violation of decency standards, something that shocks moral sensibility.
  • Indecent — similar to obscene but milder and more general. Indecent is closer to "not proper" or "not modest." Obscene is stronger and more extreme.
  • Inappropriate — a mild word meaning "not suitable for the context." Obscene is far stronger than simply inappropriate.
