  • Knives and cutting blades for butchering animals and cutting plant material
  • Scrapers for cleaning animal hides
  • Surgical tools for cutting skin, centuries before modern medicine

Obsidian was so valuable that it was traded over vast distances. Archaeologists have found obsidian tools hundreds of miles from the nearest obsidian source, proving that ancient trade networks actively transported it. Civilizations like the Aztecs in Mexico regarded it as sacred and used it in religious rituals, weapons, and even as flat, polished mirrors.

Obsidian has not been left behind by modern civilization. Surgeons performing extremely delicate operations — particularly on the eye — sometimes use obsidian scalpel blades. Because the edge is so much thinner than steel, cuts made with obsidian cause less tissue damage and leave smaller scars. The incision is so precise that surrounding cells are barely disturbed.

Beyond medicine, obsidian is widely used in:

  • Jewelry — cut and polished into beads, pendants, and cabochons (smooth, rounded gemstones)
  • Decorative objects — sculptures, figurines, and ornamental pieces
  • Crystal healing and spiritual practices — many cultures and traditions consider it a protective stone
Where It Is Found in the World

Obsidian is found wherever volcanic activity has occurred and lava cooled rapidly — especially near water, which accelerates the cooling. It is not rare, but it is not spread everywhere either.

Major natural deposits exist in:

  • The western United States (Oregon, California, Wyoming near Yellowstone)
  • Mexico and Central America
  • Iceland
  • Japan
  • Turkey (one of the oldest known sources used by ancient humans)
  • Italy (the Lipari islands)
  • Parts of East Africa and New Zealand

If you had to boil it down to one sentence: Obsidian is a naturally formed volcanic glass — usually jet black and glassy in appearance — created when lava cools almost instantly, making it capable of producing edges sharper than any metal blade, which is why humans have used it as a cutting tool from the Stone Age to modern surgery.
11261:
Something is obsolete when it is no longer used, no longer needed, or no longer relevant — because something newer, better, or more suitable has taken its place. It describes a thing that used to be useful, important, or in active use, but now has been left behind by the world.

The key idea is this: obsolete things are not just old. They are old and replaced and no longer serving their original purpose in any meaningful way.
The Heart of the Word

Think of it this way. When something becomes obsolete, the world has moved on without it. It still exists, perhaps, but it no longer has a real role to play. Nobody needs it anymore because something else now does the job better, faster, or more efficiently.

A candle is old. But a candle is not obsolete — people still use candles. A horse-drawn carriage, however, is obsolete as a form of everyday city transport. Cars came along, did the job far better, and the horse-drawn carriage was quietly retired from daily life. It didn't disappear from the Earth. It just stopped mattering in the way it once did.

That replacement is what sets "obsolete" apart from simply being old or rare.
What Can Become Obsolete?

Almost anything can become obsolete. The word is used across many areas of life.

Technology is the most common example. Floppy disks are obsolete. VHS tapes are obsolete. Dial-up internet connections are obsolete. Each of these was replaced by something that worked better — USB drives, streaming services, broadband internet. They didn't just get old; they got replaced and left behind.

Skills can become obsolete too. The skill of operating a telegraph machine, for example, is now obsolete. No company needs a telegraph operator anymore. The skill existed, it was valued, people were trained in it — and then it became irrelevant because the world no longer had a use for it.

Words and language can be obsolete. There are words in old English texts that are considered obsolete because nobody uses or understands them in modern speech anymore. They were once perfectly normal words, but language evolved and they were dropped.

Laws and rules can become obsolete. If a law was written to regulate something that no longer exists, that law is now obsolete — it technically exists on paper but serves no real function.

Ideas and methods can also become obsolete. An outdated medical practice, for example, may be considered obsolete once science has proven better methods exist.
The Process of Becoming Obsolete

Becoming obsolete is usually a gradual process, not a sudden one. Things don't typically go from "widely used" to "completely obsolete" overnight. There is often a middle stage where something is becoming obsolete — still in occasional use, but clearly fading out as people and industries shift toward something newer.

For example, physical maps are in that in-between stage right now. Many people still use them, but GPS navigation has made them largely unnecessary for most travellers. They are becoming obsolete, even if they are not fully obsolete yet.

Once something is fully obsolete, it may still exist as a collector's item, a museum piece, or a curiosity — but it no longer plays an active, functional role in everyday life.
What Obsolete Does NOT Mean

This is important, because "obsolete" is sometimes confused with nearby words.

Obsolete does not simply mean "old." Age alone does not make something obsolete. A wooden spoon is old technology, but it is not obsolete — it is still widely used and has never been replaced in any meaningful way. A 500-year-old book may still be read and valued. Age must be paired with being replaced and no longer in use for something to be called obsolete.

Obsolete does not mean "broken" or "damaged." A broken machine is not obsolete. Obsolete means it has been superseded — meaning something else has taken over its role — not that it stopped working.

Obsolete does not mean "rare" or "vintage." Some old things are treasured, collected, or considered stylish precisely because they are old. A vintage record player or a classic film camera might be rare and cherished, but people who use them would argue they still serve a real, valued purpose. Obsolete carries a sense of something being genuinely left behind, not romanticized.

Obsolete does not mean "wrong." Something can be true and yet be an obsolete way of thinking about a problem — it was simply outpaced by a better approach.
Shades of Meaning — How Strong Is the Word?

"Obsolete" is a fairly strong word. It suggests that something's time has well and truly passed — not just that it is slightly behind the times, but that it has been genuinely replaced and is no longer in active, mainstream use. It is stronger than simply saying something is "old-fashioned" or "outdated."

If something is outdated, it may still be in use but needs updating.
If something is obsolete, it is past the point of updating — the whole thing has been replaced.
Synonyms — and How They Differ

Knowing the differences between "obsolete" and its near-synonyms will sharpen your understanding:

Outdated means something is behind the current times but may still be partially in use. A website with an outdated design still works; it just hasn't kept up with modern design standards. Outdated is softer than obsolete.

Outmoded means something has gone out of fashion or is no longer considered the right or modern way of doing something. It often applies to methods, styles, or thinking. It is close to obsolete but slightly softer in tone.

Archaic means something is very ancient and belongs to a much earlier period. It is often used for language, customs, or ideas that feel extremely old. It emphasises age even more than obsolete does, and carries a sense of something being from a very distant past.

Antiquated is similar to archaic — it suggests something is so old that it feels out of place in the modern world. Both archaic and antiquated focus more on the oldness, while obsolete focuses more on the replacement and loss of function.

Defunct means something no longer exists or operates at all. A defunct company has shut down entirely. Obsolete things may still physically exist but are no longer in use; defunct things have simply stopped existing or functioning altogether. Defunct is the more final word.
Antonyms — The Opposite Ideas

To round out your understanding, here are the words that sit on the opposite end from "obsolete":

Current — in active use right now, relevant to the present moment.
Modern — of or belonging to the present time; up-to-date.
Up-to-date — fully in line with the latest developments.
Cutting-edge — at the very frontier of what is new and advanced.
Relevant — still meaningful and applicable to the present situation.
Common Ways the Word Is Used

Here are the most natural patterns you will see "obsolete" used in:

"Something becomes obsolete." — This is the most natural phrasing. Things become obsolete; they reach that condition over time.

"Something renders another thing obsolete" or "makes something obsolete." — This means one thing causes another to become obsolete. Smartphones rendered many devices obsolete — separate cameras, alarm clocks, calculators, maps, and music players all lost their necessity because one device absorbed all their roles.

"Obsolete technology / skills / methods / words." — These are the most common nouns paired with obsolete.
Example Sentences

Here are clear example sentences that show the word in natural use:

"Cassette tapes became obsolete once CDs and then digital music took over."

"Many factories now use robots, making several manual assembly jobs obsolete."

"The law was written in 1890 and is now completely obsolete — the industry it was meant to regulate has not existed for decades."

"She worried that her programming skills would become obsolete if she didn't keep learning new languages."

"GPS technology has rendered the traditional paper map largely obsolete for most travellers."

"The word 'forsooth' is considered obsolete in modern English — it was once a common expression meaning 'in truth,' but nobody uses it in everyday speech today."
The One-Line Summary
If you want to carry just one clear idea with you: obsolete means something that has been replaced by something better and is no longer in active, relevant use — it has been left behind by progress.
11262:
An obstacle is anything — a thing, a person, a situation, or even a feeling — that stands in your way and makes it harder or impossible to move forward, reach a goal, or complete something.

Think of it simply: you are trying to get somewhere or achieve something. An obstacle is whatever is blocking or slowing that path.
What Makes Something an Obstacle?

Three things define an obstacle:

  1. There is a goal or a desired direction. Someone or something is trying to move, progress, or achieve something.
  2. Something resists or blocks that movement or progress. It creates friction, delay, difficulty, or a full stop.
  3. It must be dealt with. You either overcome it, go around it, remove it, or you are stopped by it.

An obstacle doesn't have to completely stop you. It may simply slow you down or make things significantly harder — and that is still an obstacle.
Obstacles Can Be Physical or Non-Physical

This is important: the word is not limited to things you can touch.

Physical obstacles are tangible things that block literal movement:

  • A fallen tree blocking a road is an obstacle.
  • A locked door is an obstacle to entering a room.
  • A steep mountain is an obstacle to reaching the other side.

Non-physical obstacles are circumstances, conditions, or internal states that block progress or achievement:

  • Lack of money is an obstacle to starting a business.
  • Fear of failure is an obstacle to taking risks.
  • A law that forbids something is an obstacle to doing it.
  • Someone's opposition or resistance can be an obstacle to a plan.
  • Lack of education can be an obstacle to getting a good job.

The word applies equally well to both. In everyday use, non-physical obstacles are often discussed more than physical ones.
The Feeling the Word Carries (Connotation)

"Obstacle" is almost always a negative word — it signals something unwanted, something that creates difficulty or frustration. When someone says "there are many obstacles," you immediately understand that things are hard and not going smoothly.

However, the word can be used in a neutral or even inspiring way when the context is about growth, perseverance, or challenge. Athletes, coaches, and motivational speakers often talk about obstacles as things that test and strengthen you. In that sense, an obstacle is not just a problem — it is a challenge that, if overcome, makes you more capable.

But in its basic nature, the word signals resistance and difficulty.
Size and Severity

Obstacles are not all equal. They exist on a wide scale:

  • A minor obstacle is a small inconvenience — something that slows you down briefly.
  • A major obstacle is a serious challenge — something that demands real effort, time, or resources.
  • An insurmountable obstacle (or an obstacle you cannot overcome) is something so large or difficult that it may stop you entirely. "Insurmountable" means it cannot be overcome.
How "Obstacle" Is Used with Other Words (Collocations)

Learning which words naturally go with "obstacle" will help you use and understand it correctly:

Verbs commonly used with obstacle:

  • Overcome an obstacle — to successfully deal with it and move past it. (She overcame every obstacle on her way to success.)
  • Face an obstacle — to encounter or be confronted by it. (He faced many obstacles in his career.)
  • Remove an obstacle — to eliminate it so it no longer blocks the way. (The new policy removed a major obstacle for small businesses.)
  • Pose / present an obstacle — to create or represent a blockage. (The lack of funding posed a serious obstacle to the project.)
  • Hit an obstacle — to unexpectedly encounter one. (The negotiations hit an obstacle when both sides disagreed on terms.)
  • Clear an obstacle — similar to overcome; to successfully get past it. (The team cleared every obstacle to meet the deadline.)

Adjectives commonly used with obstacle:

  • A major / serious / significant obstacle — an important or difficult one.
  • A minor / small obstacle — not very serious.
  • An insurmountable obstacle — one that cannot be overcome.
  • A formidable obstacle — one that is large, powerful, or intimidating.
  • An unexpected / unforeseen obstacle — one that was not anticipated.
  • A common obstacle — one that many people face.

Prepositions used with obstacle:

  • An obstacle to something — this is the most natural pattern. (Poverty is an obstacle to education. Fear is an obstacle to growth.)
  • An obstacle in the path/way — describing something physically or figuratively blocking a route. (There was a huge obstacle in the path of progress.)
Obstacle in a Sentence — Examples

These examples show the word in real, varied contexts:

  • "Language was the biggest obstacle for immigrants trying to find work."
  • "The construction work on the main road became an obstacle for daily commuters."
  • "Self-doubt is often the greatest obstacle a person faces."
  • "The two countries agreed to remove all trade obstacles between them."
  • "Despite all the obstacles, she never gave up on her dream."
  • "His criminal record was an obstacle to getting hired."
  • "The lack of clean water is a major obstacle to development in the region."
Synonyms — and How They Differ from "Obstacle"

These words are related to "obstacle" but are not identical. Understanding the differences makes your understanding sharper:

  • Barrier — often implies something more permanent, structural, or fixed, like a wall or a system. It also suggests complete blockage rather than just difficulty. (A language barrier. Trade barriers.)
  • Hindrance — something that slows you down or makes things harder, but may not fully stop you. It feels slightly softer than "obstacle." (The rain was a hindrance, but we continued.)
  • Impediment — similar to hindrance; often used in formal or legal language. (A speech impediment. An impediment to justice.)
  • Hurdle — imagines a challenge like a hurdle in a race — something you jump over and keep going. It implies the obstacle is part of a process and can be cleared. (Getting a visa was just one of many hurdles.)
  • Stumbling block — an obstacle, often unexpected, that trips you up or causes you to fail or lose progress. The image is of literally stumbling over something. (Funding remained the key stumbling block.)
  • Difficulty — a general word for something hard; it's broader and less specific than obstacle. It doesn't necessarily imply blockage the way obstacle does.
  • Challenge — broader and more neutral than obstacle; sometimes used positively. A challenge can be an opportunity. An obstacle is more clearly negative.

So: obstacle sits at the centre — it is clear, direct, slightly formal, and applies to both physical and non-physical things. Among its synonyms, it is probably the most versatile and commonly used in writing and speech.
Antonyms — What Is the Opposite?

Words that mean the opposite of obstacle — something that helps or makes things easier:

  • Aid / Help — provides support toward a goal.
  • Advantage — something that puts you in a better position.
  • Facilitator — something that makes a process easier or smoother.
  • Boost — something that pushes you forward.
  • Enabler — something that makes a thing possible.
A Common Expression: "Obstacle Course"

An obstacle course is a physical course (often used in military training, fitness, or competitions) that is designed with many barriers, walls, tunnels, ropes, and challenges that participants must get through or past. The phrase is also used figuratively: "Applying for a visa felt like running an obstacle course" — meaning the process had many difficult steps and hurdles.
Summary in One Sentence

An obstacle is anything — physical or non-physical — that stands in the way of movement, progress, or the achievement of a goal, making it harder or impossible to succeed without dealing with it first.
11263: An obstetrician is a medical doctor who specializes in pregnancy, childbirth, and the period of time right after a baby is born.

When a woman becomes pregnant, her body goes through enormous changes over roughly nine months — and then she goes through the physically demanding process of labor and delivery. An obstetrician is the doctor trained specifically to guide and manage all of that. Their entire job revolves around making sure both the mother and the baby stay safe and healthy throughout this journey.

Think of an obstetrician as the medical expert on call for every stage of having a baby:

  • During pregnancy, they monitor the mother's health, track the baby's growth and development, order ultrasounds and tests, detect and manage complications (like high blood pressure, gestational diabetes, or unusual positioning of the baby), and advise the mother on what to eat, what to avoid, and what to expect.
  • During labor and delivery, they are the ones who step in if anything goes medically serious — whether that means performing a cesarean section (a surgical procedure to deliver the baby through an incision in the abdomen rather than vaginally), using instruments to assist delivery, or managing heavy bleeding or other emergencies.
  • After the birth (called the postpartum period), they check on the mother's recovery, manage any complications that arise from the delivery, and make sure her body is healing properly.
The branch of medicine that an obstetrician practices is called obstetrics. So "obstetrician" is simply the name for a doctor who has trained and qualified in obstetrics.

You will very frequently see the term OB/GYN (short for Obstetrics and Gynecology). This is because most obstetricians are also trained as gynecologists — doctors who handle the broader health of the female reproductive system (such as menstrual issues, ovarian cysts, fibroids, and so on) — not just pregnancy. In practice, a single doctor often does both. But the two roles are distinct:

  • The obstetrics part = pregnancy and childbirth.
  • The gynecology part = female reproductive health outside of pregnancy.

When someone says "my OB/GYN," they mean a doctor qualified in both areas. When someone specifically says "my obstetrician," they are usually referring to the pregnancy-focused aspect of that doctor's role.
How an Obstetrician Differs from a Midwife

A midwife also helps deliver babies, but is not a fully qualified medical doctor. Midwives are trained healthcare professionals who handle normal, uncomplicated pregnancies and deliveries — often focusing on a more personal, low-intervention approach. An obstetrician, being a doctor with surgical training, handles higher-risk pregnancies, complications, and situations where medical intervention is necessary. In many cases, a midwife and an obstetrician work together, with the obstetrician stepping in if something goes wrong.
When Would Someone See an Obstetrician?

• A woman who has just discovered she is pregnant will typically be referred to (or seek out) an obstetrician to manage her prenatal care.
  • A pregnant woman with a pre-existing condition (like diabetes or heart disease) will almost certainly need an obstetrician, since her pregnancy is already higher-risk.
  • During delivery at a hospital, an obstetrician is the doctor who oversees or performs the birth — especially if complications arise.
  • After giving birth, a woman follows up with her obstetrician to ensure her recovery is on track.

An obstetrician is a doctor who specializes in the medical care of women during pregnancy, through childbirth, and in the recovery period immediately after — with the training and authority to perform surgery and handle life-threatening complications if they arise.
11264:
Obstinacy is the quality of stubbornly refusing to change your opinion, decision, or behavior — even when there are very good, clear reasons to do so.

Think of it this way: imagine someone has made up their mind about something. People show them solid evidence that they are wrong. Friends reason with them. Experts advise them. And yet, that person will not budge — not even a little. That quality — that hardened, immovable refusal to reconsider — is obstinacy.

It is not just being firm. It is being unreasonably, almost defiantly firm.

This is a negative word. When you call someone's behavior "obstinacy," you are not complimenting them. You are saying their refusal to change is not justified — that a reasonable person, faced with the same facts, would have reconsidered by now.

The word carries a sense of frustration. It suggests:

  • The person is aware of the reasons to change, but ignores them.
  • Their stubbornness is making things worse.
  • Others have tried, and failed, to get through to them.

A doctor tells a patient: "You must stop eating so much salt — your blood pressure is dangerously high."

The patient says, "I've eaten this way my whole life. I'm not changing now."

The doctor explains the risks again. The family begs him. His test results worsen. Still, he refuses.

His refusal to change, despite all the evidence and pleading, is obstinacy.
How It Is Used in a Sentence

• "His obstinacy frustrated everyone on the team — he refused to consider a single suggestion."
  • "Despite the setbacks, she pushed forward with obstinacy that bordered on recklessness."
  • "The negotiations failed because of the obstinacy of both sides."
  • "The child's obstinacy in refusing to eat vegetables drove his parents to despair."

Obstinacy is not only used to describe people. It can also describe situations, problems, or conditions that resist change or refuse to improve.

For example:

  • "The obstinacy of the infection surprised the doctors — no antibiotic seemed to work."
  • "The obstinacy of the stain meant it wouldn't come out no matter how hard she scrubbed."

Here, "obstinacy" is used almost as if the thing has a stubborn will of its own. It just won't yield.
The Crucial Difference: Obstinacy vs. Determination

These two are easily confused, so this distinction matters.

Determination is admired. It means you pursue a worthy goal with strong willpower even when things get hard. The resistance is external — the world is pushing back, but you keep going. People cheer you on.

Obstinacy is criticized. It means you cling to an opinion or behavior even when logic, evidence, or wise counsel says you should change. The resistance is internal — your own mind refuses to move. People grow frustrated with you.

The key question is: Is the refusal to change reasonable, or not?

If yes → you are being determined, principled, or resilient.
If no → you are displaying obstinacy.
Closely Related Words (and How They Compare)

Stubbornness is the closest synonym. It means almost exactly the same thing and is used more casually in everyday speech. Obstinacy is slightly more formal and often implies an even stronger, more deep-seated refusal.

Inflexibility is broader — it simply means an inability or unwillingness to adapt. Obstinacy specifically involves actively resisting when pushed to change.

Intransigence is a more formal, often political synonym — it describes someone who flatly refuses to negotiate, compromise, or come to an agreement.

Mulishness and pig-headedness are informal, colorful synonyms that emphasize how irrational or animal-like the stubbornness is (as a mule is famously difficult to move).
The opposites are words like flexibility, open-mindedness, compliance, and tractability — all of which describe a willingness to listen, adapt, and change when good reasons exist.

Obstinacy is the quality of stubbornly and unreasonably refusing to change your opinion or behavior, even when faced with compelling evidence, sound advice, or strong persuasion — and this refusal is seen by others as unjustified and frustrating.
11265:
Imagine a person who has been given every good reason to change their mind — solid evidence, logical arguments, advice from people they trust — and yet, they simply refuse to budge. Not because they have a better counter-argument. Not because they know something others don't. Just because they won't. That person is obstinate.

Obstinate means stubbornly and unreasonably refusing to change your opinion, decision, or behavior, even when there are strong and sensible reasons to do so.

The single most important word in that definition is "unreasonably." This is what makes obstinate different from simply being firm or committed. A person who holds their ground because they genuinely believe they're right — and can explain why — might just be confident and principled. But a person who refuses to change even when logic, evidence, or circumstance clearly calls for it? That's obstinate.
The Tone: It's Almost Always a Criticism

When you call someone obstinate, you are criticizing them. You are saying their refusal to change is not a strength — it is a flaw that is causing problems, blocking progress, or frustrating everyone around them.

Think of it as a stronger, more serious version of "stubborn." You might jokingly call a friend stubborn for always wanting to eat at the same restaurant. But if a manager refuses to hear any feedback, ignores clear evidence that their strategy isn't working, and simply won't adapt — "stubborn" starts to feel too mild. Obstinate is the right word. It carries more weight and implies a greater degree of unreasonableness.

Here is a reliable mental test. Ask yourself two questions: First, has the person been given genuinely good reasons, evidence, or pressure to change? Second, do they still refuse — without a sound reason of their own?

If both answers are yes, the behavior is obstinate.

If the person hasn't been given good reasons yet, they aren't necessarily obstinate — they simply haven't been challenged. And if they have a solid counter-argument, they might actually be right (and everyone else might be wrong). Obstinate applies specifically when a person digs in their heels despite knowing, on some level, that they probably shouldn't.

Most commonly, it describes people and their attitudes or actions. A person can be obstinate. A refusal can be obstinate. A silence, a stance, or a response can be obstinate.

"He is an obstinate man who never listens to anyone." "Her obstinate refusal to apologize damaged the friendship." "The committee maintained its obstinate silence on the issue."

Interestingly, obstinate is also used in more formal and medical contexts to describe problems or conditions that resist treatment — things that stubbornly "refuse" to go away. "The patient suffered from an obstinate cough that lasted for weeks." "They struggled with an obstinate stain that nothing could remove." Here, the word is being applied to a non-human thing by treating it as if it were a person stubbornly refusing to yield — and it works beautifully.
How It Differs from Words That Look Similar

This is where most learners get tripped up, so pay close attention.

Determined and persistent are positive words. They describe someone who works hard and keeps going toward a goal. A determined person refuses to quit. An obstinate person refuses to change. The direction is completely different: determination is about not giving up on something worthwhile, while obstinance is about not changing when you clearly should.

Stubborn is the closest synonym, and in everyday speech the two are often used interchangeably. But obstinate is slightly stronger, more formal, and carries a clearer sense of unreasonableness. A stubborn person might just be set in their ways. An obstinate person has been given good reasons to change — and still refuses.

Tenacious is positive — it means holding on firmly and persistently to something valuable, often through hardship. You'd call a great athlete or a relentless researcher tenacious. You wouldn't call them obstinate, because obstinate implies the refusal is a problem, not a virtue.

Headstrong is similar to obstinate but leans more toward someone who charges ahead on impulse and insists on doing things their own way — often out of pride or overconfidence. Obstinate leans more toward passive refusal: planting your feet and simply not moving.

Resolute is entirely positive — it means firmly committed to a decision or cause you believe in for good reason. A resolute person is admirable. An obstinate person is frustrating.

The cleanest way to remember the difference: if someone's refusal is admirable, use determined, tenacious, or resolute. If their refusal is unreasonable and harmful, obstinate is your word.

Understanding a word's antonyms locks in its meaning. The opposite of obstinate is being open-minded, flexible, or amenable. An open-minded person genuinely considers other viewpoints. A flexible person adapts when the situation calls for it. An amenable person is willing to go along with reasonable suggestions. Other good antonyms include: agreeable, yielding, compliant, receptive, and accommodating. An obstinate person possesses none of these qualities.

"Despite repeated warnings from his doctor, the obstinate patient refused to change his unhealthy diet." He was given clear expert advice. He refused it without good reason. That's obstinate.

"The peace talks failed because both leaders were too obstinate to make even small compromises." Here, obstinate is directly the cause of a real-world failure — showing just how damaging the quality can be.

"After years of trying, scientists finally developed a cure for the obstinate disease that had resisted all previous treatments." Here, the disease is being described as if it were stubbornly holding out — the non-human use of the word.

"The obstinate child sat on the floor and refused to move, no matter what his parents said or offered." The clearest, most everyday picture of obstinate behavior.

Since you are learning this word for life, it helps to know its family. The noun form is obstinacy (or, less commonly, obstinateness) — meaning the quality or state of being obstinate: "His obstinacy cost him many friendships." The adverb form is obstinately — meaning in an obstinate manner: "She obstinately refused to hear any other opinion."
One Image to Remember It Forever

Picture a mule. Mules are famously known for planting their hooves and refusing to move, no matter how much you push, pull, or persuade. An obstinate person is that mule. They've heard you. They understand you. They just won't move — and that, precisely, is the problem.
11266:
Obstreperous means noisy, unruly, and difficult to control — all at the same time.

When you call someone or something obstreperous, you are saying two things at once:

  • They are being loud and disruptive
  • They are actively resisting control or authority

This is the heart of the word. It is never just one of those things alone. A library full of silent rule-breakers is not obstreperous. A loud, cheerful concert crowd is not obstreperous either. Obstreperous is when someone is both making noise and refusing to be managed — usually in a way that is causing problems for the people around them.

Think of it like this: someone obstreperous is not simply being difficult. They are being difficult loudly. They shout, they resist, they make a scene. There is an energy to it — almost a chaos — that makes the people around them feel like they have lost control of the situation.

Importantly, obstreperous behaviour is usually deliberate, even if the person doing it is not fully aware. It is not passive. An obstreperous child is not simply sitting in the corner and quietly refusing to eat their vegetables — they are throwing the plate and screaming about it.
Who or What Can Be Obstreperous?

The word is most commonly used to describe people, and especially:

  • Children — this is by far the most common use. A toddler having a meltdown in a supermarket, screaming and writhing on the floor, refusing every attempt to calm them down, is the classic picture of an obstreperous child.
  • Groups and crowds — a rowdy mob of protesters who drown out every speaker, shove past barriers, and ignore police instructions is an obstreperous crowd.
  • Adults in formal settings — a politician, employee, or meeting attendee who constantly interrupts, argues loudly, and refuses to follow procedure can be described as obstreperous.
  • Animals — less commonly, but a horse that kicks, bucks, and won't be saddled could be called obstreperous.

It is rarely used to describe objects or situations, and when it is, it feels like a stretch. The word lives most naturally when attached to living, breathing beings who are actively misbehaving.
The Tone and Feeling of the Word

Obstreperous carries a negative connotation, but the degree of negativity depends on context.

When used about children, the word can carry a touch of amused exasperation — the kind of feeling a grandparent might have watching a toddler be absolutely impossible, with a faint smile hidden behind a sigh. It acknowledges that the behaviour is bad, but it is not exactly outrage.

When used about adults, the word tends to be more critical and disapproving. An obstreperous adult is someone who is embarrassing themselves, disrupting others, and refusing to behave with basic dignity.

It is a fairly strong word. Here is a rough sense of the scale:

Lively → Boisterous → Rowdy → Obstreperous → Out of control

  • Boisterous means energetically noisy and enthusiastic — but in a generally positive or harmless way. Children laughing loudly and running around at a birthday party are boisterous.
  • Rowdy means noisy and disorderly — it has a negative edge, but it is milder. A rowdy pub crowd might be annoying, but they are not necessarily resisting control.
  • Obstreperous is stronger than both. It means the person is not just noisy or disorderly — they are actively pushing back against anyone trying to manage them.
How It Differs From Similar Words

Several words are close to obstreperous, but none of them are a perfect swap:

Unruly — means hard to control, but does not necessarily mean noisy. A silent child who simply refuses every instruction is unruly. That child only becomes obstreperous when they start screaming about it.

Vociferous — means expressing something loudly and forcefully (e.g., "a vociferous complaint"). It focuses purely on loudness of expression. You can be vociferous without being chaotic or resistant to control.

Turbulent — refers to disorder, conflict, and instability in a broader sense. You can describe a turbulent era in history, but you would not easily describe a toddler as turbulent.

Recalcitrant — means stubbornly resistant to authority — similar in spirit to obstreperous, but without the noise. A recalcitrant student silently refuses to do their homework. An obstreperous student loudly argues with the teacher while refusing.

Obstreperous sits in a unique position because it combines noise with resistance — it needs both to be accurate.
When Would You Actually Use This Word?

Obstreperous is a formal to semi-formal word. You would not typically hear it in casual everyday conversation — people would more naturally say "out of control," "a nightmare," or simply "rowdy" in informal speech. However, you will encounter it in:

  • Written English — newspapers, books, essays
  • Formal or professional speech
  • Descriptive storytelling, where the writer wants a precise and vivid word

Using it in casual conversation is not wrong — it just sounds deliberate and somewhat literary, which can itself be used to comic effect.

Here are examples across different situations to cement the word in your mind:

  1. "The teacher sent the obstreperous boy to the principal's office after he spent twenty minutes shouting over the lesson and tipping chairs."
  2. "The politician could not finish a single sentence — the obstreperous crowd booed every word and ignored the security staff trying to restore order."
  3. "The once-quiet meeting turned obstreperous when the CEO announced the pay cuts, and several employees began shouting over one another."
  4. "The obstreperous toddler flung herself to the floor of the toy shop, screaming, while her exhausted father tried to reason with her."
  5. "Even the most experienced dog trainer had never dealt with such an obstreperous animal — the dog barked constantly, bit through three leashes, and refused every command."
A Simple Way to Remember It

If you ever need to check yourself before using the word, ask two questions:

  1. Are they being loud and disruptive?
  2. Are they resisting control or authority?

If both answers are yes — the word fits perfectly. If only one answer is yes — reach for a different word.
Obstreperous describes someone who is noisy, chaotic, and stubbornly resistant to being controlled — someone who makes a scene and refuses to settle down no matter who tries to stop them.
11267:
To obstruct something means to get in its way and stop it — or make it much harder — from moving forward, passing through, or succeeding. Think of it as placing a barrier between something and where it's trying to go, whether that "something" is a person, a vehicle, light, or even an idea or process.

The most important thing to understand is that obstruct always implies active interference. You aren't simply failing to help — you are standing in the way, creating a problem that wouldn't exist without you.

1. Physical obstruction is the more literal sense. When something obstructs a path, a road, a pipe, a view, or an opening, it blocks that space so that movement or sight becomes difficult or impossible. A boulder that has rolled onto a highway obstructs traffic. A thick cloud obstructs sunlight. A building built right in front of a window obstructs the view. In medicine, a clot in an artery obstructs blood flow.

The key quality here is that the "blocker" sits directly in the path of something that needs to pass through.

2. Abstract or figurative obstruction is when you block a process, a plan, or a person's efforts — not physically, but by interfering with how things are supposed to work. A corrupt official who hides evidence obstructs an investigation. A politician who constantly delays votes obstructs legislation. A controlling manager who refuses to share resources obstructs a team's progress.

This second meaning is extremely common and arguably the more powerful of the two. It often carries a sense of wrongdoing — of someone deliberately getting in the way of something that is legitimate and rightful.

Obstruct doesn't always mean total, permanent blockage. It sits on a spectrum. Obstructing something can mean slowing it down significantly, making it very difficult, or stopping it entirely. What matters is that you are creating a meaningful, active obstacle — not just a minor inconvenience.

In everyday physical contexts, obstruction can be unintentional. A car that breaks down and blocks a lane is obstructing traffic, even though the driver didn't mean to. However, in legal, political, and formal contexts, "obstruct" almost always implies deliberate interference. When someone is accused of obstructing justice, the implication is that they intentionally tried to disrupt or corrupt the legal process — and in most countries, this is a serious crime.
Where You'll Commonly See It Used

In law and justice: "Obstruct justice" is one of the most well-known phrases using this word. It means deliberately interfering with the work of courts, police, or investigators — for example, by destroying evidence, lying to authorities, or pressuring witnesses.

In politics: Politicians or factions are often said to obstruct legislation, a vote, or a bill when they use procedural tricks, delays, or opposition to stop a law from being passed.

In medicine: Doctors speak of obstructed airways, obstructed bowels, or obstructed arteries, meaning something is blocking the normal flow inside the body.

In everyday life: Construction materials left on a pavement obstruct pedestrians. A tall fence obstructs a neighbour's view. A noisy crowd obstructs someone's ability to concentrate.
How It Differs From Similar Words

Block is the closest cousin. However, "block" suggests complete, total stoppage — like a wall. "Obstruct" can be partial; it makes things significantly harder without necessarily making them fully impossible.

Hinder and impede are softer. To hinder or impede something is to slow it down or make it harder, but the effect feels less forceful and less deliberate than "obstruct."

Thwart means to successfully defeat someone's plan or intention — the blocking is complete and the goal is foiled. You can obstruct someone without ultimately stopping them; if you stop them entirely, you thwart them.

Hamper means to restrict freedom of movement or action, often through many small difficulties rather than one clear barrier.

So in terms of strength: hinder / hamper → obstruct → block / thwart, roughly speaking.

"Obstruct" is a moderately formal word. It appears very often in news, legal documents, politics, and medicine. In casual speech, people are more likely to say "block" or "get in the way of," but "obstruct" is the word of choice when the situation feels serious, official, or involves some kind of wrongdoing or consequence.

Knowing the family of words built around "obstruct" will help you recognise it in different shapes:

Obstruction (noun) refers either to the act of obstructing ("the obstruction of justice") or to the thing that is doing the blocking ("remove the obstruction from the pipe").

Obstructive (adjective) describes someone or something that tends to create obstacles or gets in the way — "an obstructive colleague," "obstructive behaviour."

Obstructor (noun) is a person who obstructs.

Obstructionism (noun) refers to the deliberate, systematic practice of blocking progress — especially in politics — often as a strategy rather than a single act.
To do the opposite of obstruct is to facilitate, enable, assist, clear the way, or expedite — all of which involve making progress easier rather than harder.

If you want one clear image to anchor this word in your mind: imagine someone standing in a doorway with their arms spread wide, refusing to let anyone through. That person is obstructing passage. Now zoom out — that same image applies whether the "doorway" is a road, a legal process, a democratic vote, or a pipe in your body. Obstruct always means: something is in the way, it is causing real difficulty, and it shouldn't be there.
11268:
To obtrude means to push something — or yourself — forward into a place, a conversation, or someone's attention when it is unwanted, uninvited, or inappropriate. The thing being obtruded doesn't slip in quietly. It forces itself in, and that forcing is the whole point of the word.

Think of it this way: imagine you're having a quiet, personal conversation with a friend, and someone walks up and starts inserting themselves into it without being asked. That person is obtruding. Now imagine someone in a meeting who keeps hammering their own opinions onto everyone else, whether others want to hear them or not. They are obtruding their views. The common thread is always the same — something unwelcome is being pushed where it doesn't belong.

Obtrude works in two slightly different ways, and it helps to understand both.

1. Obtrude something on or upon someone
Here, you are forcing something — an opinion, a feeling, a presence — onto another person.

  • "She didn't wish to obtrude her personal problems upon her colleagues."
  • "He constantly obtruded his political views on anyone who would listen."
  • "The novelist was careful not to obtrude his own morals upon the story."

In all these cases, something is being pushed at someone who didn't ask for it.

2. Obtrude (on/into something) — without a direct object
Here, a person or thing is simply pushing itself into a situation where it doesn't belong.

  • "I didn't want to obtrude on their grief."
  • "A loud noise obtruded on the silence of the room."
  • "He felt uncomfortable obtruding into their private moment."

Here, nothing is being handed to anyone specifically — the person or thing is just forcing its way into a space where it's out of place.

This is what truly separates obtrude from just saying "interrupt" or "intrude."

Obtrude carries a strong sense of unwanted forcefulness. There's a slight air of tactlessness about it — whoever or whatever is obtruding is being too pushy, too present, too loud, too visible in a situation that called for restraint or quiet. It suggests that the thing obtruding is crossing a line of social or emotional appropriateness.

Importantly, the person obtruding may not always mean to be rude. Sometimes they are simply unaware that they are forcing themselves into an unwelcome position. The word doesn't always assign bad intent — but it does always assign an unwanted effect.

You can also use it when talking about physical things, not just people or opinions. A building that blocks a beautiful view obtrudes on the landscape. An ugly advertisement obtrudes on an otherwise peaceful scene. The idea is the same — something is pushing itself into a space in a way that is jarring and unwelcome.

Obtrude sits at a particular level of intrusiveness. It is stronger than simply being present where you shouldn't be, but it isn't as aggressive as outright forcing or barging in violently. The closest everyday word to it is intrude, but obtrude places heavier emphasis on the pushing, thrusting quality of the act — the sense that the unwanted thing is actively making itself prominent or noticeable. Intrusion is often just being somewhere you shouldn't; obtruding is being there loudly or insistently.

Obtrude is a formal and literary word. You will encounter it more often in careful writing — novels, essays, formal speeches — than in casual everyday conversation. If you use it in speech, it will sound educated and deliberate. In writing, it is precise and elegant. It lets you say, in a single word, that something is unwelcome, forceful, inappropriate, and intrusive — all at once.

All of these come from the same root idea:

  • Obtrusive (adjective) — Noticeable in an unwanted, irritating way. "The flashing advertisement was obtrusive and distracting." Something obtrusive keeps pushing itself into your attention when you'd rather it didn't.
  • Unobtrusive (adjective) — The opposite. Something that stays quietly in the background, not drawing unwanted attention to itself. "The waiter was efficient and unobtrusive." This is actually one of the most commonly used forms of the word family.
  • Obtrusively (adverb) — In a manner that is obtrusive. "He laughed obtrusively during the solemn ceremony."
  • Obtrusion (noun) — The act of obtruding. "She resented the obtrusion of outside noise into her reading time."
The Single Sentence to Remember It By

If you ever need to anchor the word in your memory, hold onto this:

To obtrude is to push yourself — or something — into a space where you are not welcome and were not invited, in a way that is noticeable and unwanted.

Everything else about the word flows from that core.
11269:
Something obtrusive forces itself on your attention in a way that feels unwanted, excessive, or out of place. It is noticed not because it is beautiful or interesting, but because it is too much — too loud, too visible, too pushy, or simply present in a place where it shouldn't be.

Think of it this way: imagine you're watching a movie and a huge logo is plastered right in the middle of the screen the whole time. It's not there to help you — it just gets in the way. That logo is obtrusive. It demands your attention without earning it, and it disrupts your experience in the process.

The word carries a feeling of intrusion and excess. Something obtrusive doesn't ask permission to be noticed — it shoves itself forward.
Two Main Ways the Word is Used

"Obtrusive" applies to things and to people, and the meaning is consistent across both — something/someone that sticks out too much or pushes itself where it isn't wanted.

1. Obtrusive things

This is the more common use. Something obtrusive is visually, audibly, or generally too prominent for the situation. It draws attention to itself and away from everything else, and this feels disruptive rather than pleasing.

  • A tiny, tasteful sign outside a restaurant is fine. A massive, flashing neon sign in a quiet residential street is obtrusive — it dominates everything around it and feels out of place.
  • Pop-up advertisements that suddenly cover the article you're trying to read are obtrusive. They interrupt your experience forcefully.
  • A small, subtle scar might go unnoticed. A large, vivid one right on someone's face might be described as obtrusive because it immediately draws the eye, whether you intend to look at it or not.
  • Loud construction noise in a peaceful library is obtrusive — it barges in and makes itself impossible to ignore.

Notice a pattern: something obtrusive makes itself the center of attention against your will. You didn't choose to notice it. It forced itself on you.

2. Obtrusive people (or behaviour)

A person who is obtrusive pushes themselves into spaces, conversations, or situations where they are not welcome or needed. They don't read social cues. They interrupt, impose, or make their presence felt too strongly.

  • A neighbour who walks into your home unannounced and starts offering unsolicited opinions about your furniture is being obtrusive.
  • A salesperson who follows you around a shop, hovering over your shoulder and talking constantly even after you've said you're just browsing, is being obtrusive.
  • Someone who keeps interrupting a private conversation between two people to insert their own opinions is obtrusive.

For people, the word overlaps with being intrusive or pushy, but "obtrusive" specifically emphasizes the sense that the person is making themselves too visible or present — taking up too much social space.
The Key Feeling the Word Captures

The emotion that "obtrusive" triggers in the person experiencing it is usually mild irritation, discomfort, or distraction. It's not necessarily offensive or harmful — it's just in the way. It creates friction. It makes things harder to enjoy, use, or appreciate because it keeps drawing your focus to itself.

A good test: if something makes you think "I wish that weren't there" or "I wish they'd tone it down" — you're probably dealing with something obtrusive.

The most important word to learn alongside "obtrusive" is its direct opposite: unobtrusive.

Something unobtrusive blends in smoothly. It does its job without calling attention to itself. It doesn't interrupt. It doesn't stick out. It is subtle and modest.

  • A small, tasteful watermark on a photo is unobtrusive — you can see it if you look, but it doesn't distract from the image.
  • Background music in a café that you barely notice is unobtrusive — it adds to the atmosphere without dominating it.
  • A quiet, professional assistant who anticipates your needs without hovering is unobtrusive.

Unobtrusive = present but not pushy. Obtrusive = too present, too pushy.

Understanding the two as a pair will lock both words into your memory.

These words are close in meaning to "obtrusive," but each has a slightly different shade:

  • Intrusive — focuses on the sense of invading a private or personal space. It's slightly stronger and more personal than "obtrusive." (An intrusive question is one that feels like it crosses a personal boundary.)
  • Conspicuous — simply means "very noticeable." It's neutral on its own — something can be conspicuous in a good way. Obtrusive, by contrast, is always somewhat negative.
  • Glaring — focuses on something being so obvious it can't be ignored, often used for flaws or mistakes. ("A glaring error.")
  • Pushy — used mostly for people; emphasizes excessive force and persistence, but doesn't carry the sense of visibility that obtrusive does.
  • Garish — specifically about visuals being tastelessly loud or over-the-top in colour or design.

Of all of these, "obtrusive" is the most versatile — it works for things, sounds, people, designs, behaviours, and more.

1. Obtrusive ≠ just "noticeable."
Something can be very noticeable and not obtrusive at all — a stunning painting in a gallery is hard to miss, but it belongs there. Obtrusive implies the visibility is unwanted or excessive for the context.

2. Context matters enormously.
The same thing can be obtrusive in one setting and perfectly fine in another. Loud music at a nightclub is expected. The same music at a funeral is horribly obtrusive. The word is always about whether something fits the situation — and obtrusive things don't.

3. It's always mildly negative.
Unlike "prominent" or "noticeable," "obtrusive" always carries a critical or disapproving tone. If you call something obtrusive, you're implying it should dial itself back.

Obtrusive means standing out or pushing in too much in a way that is unwanted, distracting, or out of place. It applies to things that are too visible, sounds that are too loud, or people who are too forward. The core feeling is: this is getting in the way, and I wish it wouldn't.

Its opposite, unobtrusive, means subtle, quiet, and not calling attention to itself.
11270: "Obtuse" has two distinct meanings as an adjective — one used in everyday language, and one used in mathematics. Both are equally standard and important to know.
Meaning 1: Slow or Unwilling to Understand

In everyday language, obtuse describes a person — or their behavior — as being slow to understand something, or as failing to grasp what should be reasonably clear. When you call someone obtuse, you are saying they don't "get it." They miss the point, fail to read the room, or simply cannot comprehend what is being plainly said or shown to them. The word is a criticism, and it carries a tone of frustration or impatience from the speaker.

"He was so obtuse that he didn't realize everyone at the table was uncomfortable."
"Stop being obtuse — the instructions couldn't be clearer."
"Her obtuse response to the complaint made the situation worse."

How is "obtuse" different from "stupid"?

This distinction is important. Stupid implies a general, lasting lack of intelligence — it's a broad label about someone's overall mental ability. Obtuse is more situational. It describes a specific failure to understand something in a given context, often something that a reasonable person would grasp without much difficulty. Even an otherwise intelligent, educated person can be described as obtuse in a particular moment or on a particular topic. Think of it this way: stupid is about capability, obtuse is about comprehension failing in the moment.

Can "obtuse" mean deliberately not understanding?

Yes — and this is one of the word's most important nuances. Obtuse can describe someone who is genuinely slow to understand something, but it can also describe someone who is pretending not to understand. A person might act obtuse to avoid a difficult conversation, dodge accountability, or simply be stubborn and uncooperative. In this second sense, the accusation is sharper still: the person could understand if they chose to, but they're refusing. This is why calling someone obtuse feels more pointed than calling them confused. Confusion is innocent. Obtuseness — especially in this deliberate sense — implies a kind of resistance or willful dullness.

Tone and register:

Obtuse is a moderately formal word. You're more likely to encounter it in writing, intellectual conversation, or formal settings than in casual everyday speech. When someone uses it, it often signals educated frustration — the kind a teacher might feel toward a student who refuses to engage, or a professional might feel toward an evasive colleague.
Meaning 2: In Geometry — An Obtuse Angle

In mathematics, obtuse has a precise technical meaning. An obtuse angle is any angle that measures more than 90 degrees but less than 180 degrees.

To put this in context: a right angle is exactly 90°, like the perfectly square corner of a room. An acute angle is anything less than 90° — it's sharp and narrow, like the tip of a very pointy triangle. An obtuse angle sits between those two extremes. It's wider than a right angle but hasn't opened up far enough to become a straight line (which would be exactly 180°).

A helpful real-world image: imagine slowly pushing a door open. When the door is perpendicular to the wall, that's a right angle — 90°. Push it further open to, say, 120° or 150°, and the angle between the door and the wall is now obtuse. It's wide and blunt, not sharp.

By extension, an obtuse triangle is a triangle in which one of its three interior angles is greater than 90°. Since a triangle's three angles must always add up to exactly 180°, a triangle can have at most one obtuse angle.

It might seem strange that the same word describes both a personality trait and a type of angle, but both meanings share one underlying idea: the opposite of sharp.

An obtuse angle is wide and blunt — not pointed. An obtuse person is mentally blunt — not sharp or quick in their understanding. In both cases, the word captures the quality of lacking sharpness, whether you're measuring a geometric angle or describing someone's failure to catch on. Once you see this connection, the word becomes intuitive and easy to remember.

Obtuse (describing a person or behavior): slow to understand, mentally dull, or deliberately unwilling to grasp what is being communicated. The implication is always that understanding should be within reach, which is what makes the failure — or refusal — so frustrating.

Obtuse (in geometry): an angle greater than 90° but less than 180°. A triangle containing such an angle is called an obtuse triangle.
11271:
The simplest way to understand obverse is this: it is the front face of something, specifically the face that is considered the principal, more important, or more prominent side — as opposed to the back.

Think of a coin. It has two sides. One side shows a face, a head, or the main official design. That is the obverse. The other side — the back, often showing a building, an animal, or a number — is called the reverse. In everyday language, you likely know these as "heads" and "tails." The heads side is the obverse.

So: obverse = the primary front face.
The Three Contexts Where You'll Meet This Word

The word obverse appears in three main situations. Each one builds on the same core idea.

1. Coins, Medals, and Seals (The Most Common Use)

This is where the word lives most naturally. On any official coin or medal, the obverse is the side bearing the primary image — almost always a portrait, a monarch's head, a national emblem, or the most important design the issuing authority wants to show the world.

A few things that define an obverse in this context:

  • It typically carries the date, the name of the country, or an inscription identifying the issuing authority.
  • It is defined by official convention — the government or institution decides which side is the obverse.
  • On most American coins, for example, the obverse shows a president's portrait.
  • On many British coins, the obverse shows the reigning monarch's effigy.

One important point: the obverse is not just "whichever side you happen to be looking at." It is a fixed, officially designated side. You cannot flip a coin and suddenly decide the tails side is the obverse. The designation is set.

2. General Use — The "Other Side of the Same Thing"

In broader, more general language, obverse means the natural counterpart or complement of something — the other face of the same reality.

Here is the key idea: when two things are two sides of the same coin (quite literally, as a concept), one is the obverse of the other. They are inseparable. You cannot have one without the other. They are not opposites that conflict — they are two expressions of the same single truth, just viewed from different angles.

For example:

  • Freedom and responsibility are often called two sides of the same coin. You could say: "Responsibility is the obverse of freedom" — meaning that wherever freedom exists, responsibility is right there on the other face of it, as a natural and necessary counterpart.
  • A teacher's privilege of authority has its obverse: the duty of care for students.

The word in this sense carries a feeling of philosophical pairing — not contradiction, but completion. Two faces, one thing.

3. Logic and Philosophy (Formal Use)

In formal logic, obverse has a precise technical meaning. It refers to a statement derived from another statement by negating both the predicate and the quality of the original.

Don't let that sound scary. Here's what it means in plain terms:

You take a logical statement, switch it from positive to negative (or negative to positive), and also negate the predicate. The result is the obverse, and it means exactly the same thing as the original — it is logically equivalent.

Example:

  • Original statement: "All dogs are mammals."
  • Its obverse: "No dogs are non-mammals."

Both statements say the same thing. The obverse is simply another way of expressing the identical truth. This operation — creating the obverse — is called obversion.

One more example:

  • Original: "No fish are mammals."
  • Obverse: "All fish are non-mammals."

Again — same meaning, just reworded through logical structure. In this context, the obverse is not a "side of an object" but a mirror-statement that is the logical counterpart of the original.
How Obverse Differs from Words That Look Similar

It is worth clarifying how obverse sits alongside words you might confuse it with.

Reverse is simply the back side — the opposite of the obverse. Where the obverse is the face, the reverse is the back. These two words are direct partners.

Converse (especially in logic) is different from obverse. The converse of a statement switches the subject and the predicate around. The obverse negates them. These are distinct logical operations.

Inverse involves a fuller negation of both parts. Again, a different operation from obverse.

Across all its uses, obverse always points to the same underlying idea: the front face, the principal side, or the natural and inseparable counterpart. Whether you are holding a coin, making a philosophical point about how two ideas are forever linked, or constructing a logical statement — the word obverse always signals that you are looking at one face of something that has two faces, and that this face is the primary, complementary, or structurally paired one.

A useful mental shortcut to carry with you: whenever you hear obverse, think — "the other face of the same thing, especially the main face."
11272:
To obviate something means to remove a problem, risk, or need entirely — usually by doing something in advance — so that the issue never has to be dealt with at all.

It is not about fixing a problem after it appears. It's about making the problem unnecessary, irrelevant, or non-existent before it gets a chance to cause trouble.

Think of it this way: instead of putting out a fire, you remove the fuel so the fire can never start.
The Subtlest and Most Important Point

"Obviate" is almost always used with words like need, necessity, risk, problem, or difficulty. The thing being obviated is not the final bad outcome itself — it's the need to deal with something.

Compare these two sentences:

  • "The surgery fixed the problem." → The problem existed. Then it was solved.
  • "The new treatment obviated the need for surgery." → Surgery was going to be necessary. But now, because of the new treatment, surgery is no longer needed at all. The need itself has been eliminated.

That last sentence captures the essence of the word perfectly.

Each of these shows the word doing something slightly different, so read them carefully:

"A clear contract obviates future disputes."
By writing a thorough contract now, you remove the situation where a dispute could ever arise. The dispute doesn't get resolved — it never gets a chance to exist.

"Backing up your files obviates the risk of losing your work."
The risk of losing data is made irrelevant before any data loss actually happens.

"Their early agreement on the terms obviated the need for lengthy negotiations."
Because they agreed early, long negotiations simply never had to happen.

"Good lighting in the office obviates eyestrain."
Proper lighting eliminates the problem before it becomes a problem.

In every case, notice the structure: something you do → removes the need or occasion for something unpleasant.

You will almost always see "obviate" followed by phrases like:

  • obviate the need for (the most common by far)
  • obviate the necessity of
  • obviate the risk of
  • obviate the problem of
  • obviate the difficulty of

If you remember only one phrase, remember "obviate the need for." That alone will cover 80% of real-world usage.
How It Differs From Similar Words

These words are close but not identical, and understanding the differences sharpens your grasp of "obviate."

Prevent is the broadest of the group. You can prevent a fire, a cold, a war, a mistake. "Prevent" simply means to stop something from happening. It doesn't carry the specific flavour of removing a need or an occasion for something — it just means stopping. Obviate is more specific.

Preclude means to make something impossible or to rule it out completely. It implies a hard, often formal barrier. "His past record precludes him from holding office." The difference: preclude makes something impossible; obviate makes something unnecessary. These are not the same thing.

Avert is used specifically for crises, disasters, or dangerous situations — you avert a catastrophe, a war, a tragedy. It also implies a last-minute or dramatic turning away. Obviate is calmer and more proactive, and it works for minor inconveniences just as well as major risks.

Eliminate simply means to get rid of something entirely. It doesn't imply anticipation or foresight, and it doesn't carry the specific idea of making something unnecessary. Obviate always has that forward-looking, preventive quality.

The cleanest summary: obviate = to make something unnecessary by acting beforehand.
The Register: When and Where People Use This Word

"Obviate" is a formal word. You will encounter it most in academic writing, legal documents, medical and scientific texts, business reports, and formal speeches or essays.

In everyday conversation, people rarely say "obviate." They're more likely to say "we won't need to," or "this removes the need for," or simply "this prevents."

But in formal writing and reading — which is precisely where your vocabulary matters most — "obviate" appears regularly. Knowing it will help you both understand texts where it appears and use it precisely when your own writing calls for an elevated, formal tone.

Before using the word, ask yourself: "Am I describing how something removes the need for — or the occasion for — something else, ideally by acting in advance?"

If the answer is yes, "obviate" is the right word. If you're describing fixing something after the fact, or just stopping something without that sense of making it unnecessary, choose a different word.
11273:
Something is obvious when it is so easy to see, notice, or understand that it requires almost no mental effort at all. It is right in front of you — clear, immediate, and unmistakable. You do not have to search for it, think hard about it, or analyze it. It simply presents itself to you.

Think of it this way: if you walk into a room and a fire alarm is blaring, it is obvious that something is wrong. You do not need to investigate. You do not need to be told. The conclusion arrives on its own, instantly.

Something is obvious when the gap between the thing and your understanding of it is almost zero. There is no hidden layer, no complexity to peel back, no confusion standing between you and the meaning.

There are two main ways something can be obvious:

1. Obvious to the senses — you can directly see, hear, or observe it without difficulty.

  • The stain on the white shirt is obvious.
  • The broken window is obvious.
  • The fact that someone is crying is obvious.

2. Obvious to the mind — the conclusion, answer, or meaning is so straightforward that it takes no reasoning to reach it.

  • If you eat too much sugar, the obvious consequence is feeling unwell.
  • If someone asks "What is 2 + 2?", the answer is obvious.
  • If a company loses all its customers, it is obvious that it will struggle.

In both cases, the key idea is the same: no effort is needed to perceive or understand it.

Not everything is either completely obvious or completely hidden. Obviousness exists on a sliding scale.

Something can be:

  • Blindingly obvious — so clear that it is almost impossible to miss. (Sometimes people also say glaringly obvious or patently obvious for this level of intensity.)
  • Fairly obvious — pretty clear, though perhaps not instantly.
  • Not entirely obvious — there is some work needed to see or understand it.

The word "obvious" on its own typically describes something toward the clearer end of this scale — easy enough to notice or understand without any real effort.
A Crucial Nuance: Obvious to Whom?

This is one of the most important things to understand about this word. What is obvious to one person may not be obvious to another. Obviousness is not absolute — it depends on knowledge, experience, and context.

For example:

  • The solution to a complex math problem is obvious to a mathematics professor, but not to a ten-year-old child.
  • The signs of engine trouble are obvious to a mechanic, but invisible to someone who knows nothing about cars.
  • That two people in a movie are falling in love might be obvious to an adult viewer, but completely missed by a young child watching the same film.

So when you describe something as obvious, you are always, at least implicitly, answering the question: obvious to whom?

The word "obvious" is mostly neutral, but it carries a social weight that you should be aware of. Depending on how it is used, it can have a slightly negative or dismissive tone.

When you call something obvious, you are suggesting it should already be known, seen, or understood. This can sometimes feel condescending — as if you are implying the other person should have noticed or figured it out already.

For example:

  • "The answer is obvious" — This is a neutral, factual statement.
  • "Isn't it obvious?" — This carries a slight edge. It implies that the person you are speaking to should have already known this, and perhaps they are being a little slow.
  • "That's a bit obvious, isn't it?" — Said about someone's idea, this gently criticizes it for lacking originality or depth.

This is why you sometimes hear the phrase "state the obvious" — meaning to say something that everyone already knows, which is often considered unnecessary or even slightly embarrassing.

Learning a word fully means learning how it lives in real sentences and expressions. Here are the most important ones:

"It is obvious that..." — used to introduce a fact or conclusion that needs no proof.
It is obvious that the team worked very hard on this project.

"The obvious answer / choice / solution" — used when one answer stands out above all others without much thought needed.
The obvious solution to the traffic problem is to build a new road.

"For obvious reasons" — used when the speaker thinks the reasons do not need to be spelled out because they are so clear.
For obvious reasons, the meeting was cancelled after the storm.

"State the obvious" — to say something that is already well known or visible to everyone.
I know I'm stating the obvious, but we really need more time.

"Painfully obvious" — so clear that it becomes almost awkward or uncomfortable.
It was painfully obvious that she did not want to be there.

"Blindingly / glaringly / patently obvious" — intensifiers used to emphasize just how clear something is.
It is glaringly obvious that something has gone wrong.

Several words share similar meanings with "obvious," but each has a slightly different shade.

Clear — the most general synonym. Something is clear when it is easy to understand or perceive. "Obvious" and "clear" are very close, but "clear" is slightly softer and less emphatic.

Evident — suggests that something is made clear by visible signs or evidence around you. It was evident from his expression that he was upset. Slightly more formal than "obvious."

Apparent — means something that appears or seems to be true based on what you can observe. It has a slight quality of "seeming true on the surface." The damage was apparent as soon as we arrived.

Plain — simple and easy to understand, with no confusion. The instructions were plain and easy to follow. "Plain" has a stronger connection to simplicity.

Self-evident — something so clear that it proves itself without needing any argument or demonstration. It is self-evident that all people deserve to be treated with dignity. This is more formal and philosophical than "obvious."

Manifest — very formal, often used in writing. Means clearly visible or shown. His anxiety was manifest in the way he kept checking his watch.

Among all these, "obvious" is the most everyday, most direct, and most commonly used word for the idea of something being immediately easy to see or understand.

Understanding what a word is not helps cement its meaning.

Subtle — not easy to notice; requires careful attention to detect. A subtle difference is one that is easy to miss.

Hidden — kept out of sight; not visible.

Obscure — unclear, hard to understand, or not widely known.

Ambiguous — can be understood in more than one way; not clear.

Elusive — difficult to find, understand, or achieve.

Complex / complicated — made up of many parts, requiring thought to untangle.

If something is obvious, it is none of these things.

Here is the simplest possible summary you can carry with you:

Obvious means: requiring no effort to see, notice, or understand. The meaning or truth of something is right there in front of you — immediate, clear, and unmistakable.

And the deeper understanding:

  • It exists on a spectrum — some things are more obvious than others.
  • It is always relative to a person's knowledge and experience.
  • It can carry a slightly dismissive tone depending on how it is used.
  • It is not the same as "simple" — something can be obvious without being simple, and simple without being obvious. But the two often go together.

Once you truly own this word, you will notice it everywhere — in conversations, in writing, in arguments, in everyday life — because what is easy to perceive and what requires effort is something humans are always, constantly, navigating.
11274:
Obviously means in a way that is easy to see, understand, or notice — so clear that it needs no explanation.

When you say something "obviously" happened, you are saying: any reasonable person looking at this situation would immediately see that it is true. There is no doubt. No explanation is needed. It is right in front of you.

Think of it this way: if a window is broken and a football is lying on the floor next to it, you would say "someone obviously kicked a football through the window." You did not see it happen. But the evidence makes it so plain and clear that there is no need to argue or explain — the conclusion announces itself.
The Core Feeling Behind the Word

The heart of "obviously" is the idea of no effort required to understand something. It is the opposite of something hidden, confusing, or requiring deep thought.

Imagine a signpost that is so large, so bright, and so clearly written that absolutely nobody could miss it. That is what "obviously" points to — information that is impossible to miss, like that signpost.
How It Works in a Sentence

"Obviously" is an adverb. This means it adds information about how something is true, or it signals the speaker's attitude toward the truth of a statement. It does not describe a noun. It modifies the whole sentence, or a verb, or an adjective.

Position 1 — At the beginning of a sentence:
This is the most common and natural position. It tells the listener: what I am about to say is self-evident.

Obviously, the match was cancelled — it had been raining for three days straight.
Obviously, she was upset. You could see the tears on her face.

Position 2 — In the middle of a sentence:
Here it sits between the subject and the main verb, or after a helping verb.

He obviously forgot about the meeting — his chair was empty.
She has obviously worked very hard for this.
They obviously didn't read the instructions.

Position 3 — At the end of a sentence:
Less common, but possible. It adds emphasis after the fact.

He was lying, obviously.
She knew the answer already, obviously.

All three positions carry the same meaning. The difference is only about where you want to place your emphasis.

1. Describing something that is visually or logically clear

This is the neutral, factual use. You are simply noting that something is plainly evident from the facts.

The building was obviously very old — the walls were crumbling.
